title: Jack Cressall Writing ‘Camp Justice’ Pilot Based On John Ryan Book ‘America’s Trial: Torture And The 9/11 Case’
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Ted Sarandos Shrugs Off U.S. Troubles To Mark Netflix’s 10 Years In Korea ‘Wentworth: Halfway Home’: Grace Chow & Nadine Garner Among 9 Joining Cast; Watch Trailer International Insider: Turmoil At Netflix; MIA Market Report; Patrick Brammall Interview View All October 27, 2026 8:07am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Naomi Harvey, Jack Cressall and John Ryan; 'America's Trial' (inset) Courtesy EXCLUSIVE: The TV adaptation of John Ryan ‘s non-fiction book America’s Trial: Torture and the 9/11 Case now has a writer. British screenwriter Jack Cressall is writing a pilot for Camp Justice , which will be based on Ryan’s non-fiction book from last year. Naomi Harvey from Golden Possum Productions has developed the book for TV and is attached to produce, with a U.S. co-producer being sought. It was previously with Clockwork Films, as we reported last year when Ryan’s book published. The series will explore the ongoing legal proceedings against the alleged architects of the 9/11 attacks at Guantánamo Bay, and per the synopsis will delve into “the complex legal and political landscape surrounding one of the most consequential cases in modern American history.” Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Daveigh Chase's Former Manager Vehemently Disputes GoFundMe Claims: "There Are No Medical Bills To Be Paid Or Funeral Expenses" Casting Sosie Bacon Set As Co-Lead Alongside Nikolaj Coster-Waldau In MGM+ Series 'The Black Tapes' Veteran legal affairs journalist Ryan wrote his book after spending a decade reporting from Guantánamo Bay in Cuba, exploring the post-9/11 interrogation program, the consequences of which are still playing out in court more than two decades after the events. The series will look into “justice and accountability and what happens when a nation’s pursuit of both becomes entangled with its own actions.” Ryan said: “Having Guantánamo Bay as my second home for a decade has been the reporting experience of a lifetime. The setting is surreal and the events are the literal definition of stranger than fiction. That’s why I got hooked, despite the costs to my personal life. I’m excited that more people will have a window into what goes on behind closed doors and can experience this bizarre place through Jack’s writing.” Scott Z. Burns’ film The Report , starring Adam Driver, covered similar ground, but was focused on the machinery of the interrogation program. Cressall’s debut short film, My Type , starred Sadie Stanley and Jacob Ward, with Daniel Ruah directing. It premiered at the Santa Barbara International Film Festival this year. He is developing a slate of feature films, including Destemido , a biographical drama about Brazilian big-wave surfer Marcelo Luna, and Dream Car Wash , a coming-of-age drama. For British producer Harvey and her Golden Possum operation, Camp Justice is the latest following an option for the life rights of Cuban baseball player Julio Estrada and development of a series based on John Romero, the godfather of first-person shooter whose titles including Doom , Wolfenstein 3D and Quake . “John’s book offers a rare window into life at Camp Justice,” said Harvey. “In a world where almost everything is captured on camera and shared instantly, one of the most consequential murder trials in modern history is unfolding largely out of public view. “John takes us inside a bizarre, almost surreal ecosystem where grieving families, defence lawyers, prosecutors and accused terrorists coexist on a tropical island where the makeshift court and camp x-ray co-exist with a crazy golf course, tiki bar and gitmo gift shop.” Cressall is managed by Eric Ziech at Untamed Artists LA. title: ‘Until the Day Ends’ Review: Two People Connect Across a Political Divide in a Striking Serbian Youth Drama
full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 7:44am PT ‘Until the Day Ends’ Review: Two People Connect Across a Political Divide in a Striking Serbian Youth Drama Docmaker Jelena Maksimović's first fiction feature is a narratively sparse but atmospherically throbbing exercise, playing in competition at Tokyo following its Venice Orizzonti premiere. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Until the Day Ends’ Review: Two People Connect Across a Political Divide in a Striking Serbian Youth Drama 30 minutes ago ‘Love Language’ Review: Chloë Grace Moretz Sells Words of Affirmation in an Old-School Romcom With Gen-Z Trappings 3 days ago ‘Clayface’ Review: DC Comics Horror Movie Is Good, Gross Fun, With No Franchise Homework Required 6 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Paul Spengemann Amid the turmoil of mass student protests in the streets of Belgrade, two young people are bonded by a rash act of rebellion, despite their outwardly incompatible ideologies. The premise of Serbian writer-director Jelena Maksimović ‘s “ Until the Day Ends ” portends a tidy political parable — a sort of “why can’t we all get along” homily for an age, and particularly a generation, of vastly polarized beliefs. The execution, thankfully, is flintier and more complicated than that. The film’s teachings, if any, are ambiguous, and learned on the run: Maksimović’s first fiction feature is most memorable for its galloping formal restlessness, moving at the breathless pace of its characters as they evade authority and chase a glimmer of hope in their joint resistance. Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Having made an impression on the docfest circuit with her two nonfiction features “Taurunum Boy” (2019) and “Homelands (2020), Maksimović brings a street-level, vérité -style grit to the lean narrative of “Until the Day Ends” that feels authentically keyed into the reality of current youth unrest in Eastern Europe. The film is set against a surge of real-life anti-government demonstrations in Serbia in early 2025, triggered by the tragic deaths of 16 people the previous year, following the collapse of a train station canopy in Novi Sad. But if the honest performances of a mostly non-professional ensemble contribute to a docudrama spirit, the filmmaker and her DP Paul Spengemann embrace an aesthetic of epic escapism, with roving, kinetic camerawork punctuated with enough bursting lens flare to make Janusz Kaminski blush. It’s an attention-grabbing approach that promises bigger things from Maksimović, and is propelling the film some distance on the international festival circuit. A premiere last month in Venice’s Horizons program has since been followed with berths in Vienna, Hamburg and, now, the main competition in Tokyo. The film opens on a virtuoso long take, roaming through the shadowed, disheveled hallways of a university building that, ahead of the revolution, has become something of a campsite for displaced, rebellious students; insurgent streaks of red disrupt the general gloom of the mise-en-scène. Through this faintly apocalyptic scene, we follow 20-year-old Lena (riveting newcomer Lena Trifunović), a firebrand student activist who is all in on the protests, unwavering in her anti-authoritarian conviction. That may earn her the admiration of her college comrades, but at home, she’s seen as an idealistic naif — mocked, in particular, by her older brother Milan (Miodrag Dragicevic), who is staunchly right-wing in his sympathies. Milan’s similarly inclined friends join in the teasing, but one does so with a little less gusto: 22-year-old Stefan (Andrija Krivokapić) is a working-class punk who goes with the flow of his social group, but doesn’t seem wholehearted in his pro-government stance. Perhaps sensing his lack of commitment, Lena taunts him back. This hint of connection between them is later made concrete when, at the demonstration, the two are complicit in an act of defiance — throwing a cobblestone at a policeman, badly injuring him — and must skip town for the night. As they flee, their mutual attraction deepens, but they must also parse their political differences. There’s no great capitulation or come-to-Jesus moment here, however. “Until the Day Ends” isn’t an outright romance, or a tale of a proud, gathering storm of resistance; rather, it finds human emotions and obligations sometimes messily at odds with social and political ideals. Narratively, the momentum crests at the protest, abetted by Maksimović’s most dynamic cinematic trickery — which extends to a shot from the perspective of the errant, offending stone. As a more intimate two-hander in the second half, the film is less urgent, but kept compelling by the push-pull chemistry between its two punchy young leads, playing characters who are alike in their combative vulnerability, but little more than that. Trifunović, in particular, is a real find, unpredictable in her coiled-up physicality and alternately commanding and petulant presence. Lena bristles with angry, frustrated optimism, recognizable to anyone who has ever, at one point or another, felt alone in trying to change the world. ‘Until the Day Ends’ Review: Two People Connect Across a Political Divide in a Striking Serbian Youth Drama Reviewed at Soho Screening Rooms, London, Aug. 20, 2026. title: Netflix Grapples With Digital-Ad Squeeze Amid Widening Glut of Streaming Commercials
full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 7:40am PT Netflix Grapples With Digital-Ad Squeeze Amid Widening Glut of Streaming Commercials By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Netflix Grapples With Digital-Ad Squeeze Amid Widening Glut of Streaming Commercials 32 minutes ago Billy Bob Thornton Examines Mayflower Voyage in Fox Nation Documentary Series 42 minutes ago Lisa Ling Signs With CAA 21 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Illustration: Michael Starbuck/Variety VIP+ Netflix blazed a path in the streaming era that many of its media rivals have tried to follow. As it has tried to navigate Madison Avenue, however, the company has found bumps in the road. The streaming giant last week rolled back its projections for advertising revenue, calling for $2.7 billion instead of $3 billion by the end of 2026. At a time when marketers have been moving their dollars from linear TV to streaming video by the millions, the disclosure was surprising. Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters cited “some delays in the rollout and partner integrations” for some of its new advertising products as a primary culprit for the pared-back estimates. Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Media buyers, however, say Netflix has for months held lofty expectations that are out of sync with the general advertising market. These executives say Netflix’s pricing for inventory remains too high, the process for accessing some of its inventory is too removed from the rest of the market, and that the company’s interest in selling ad-supported sports events like Christmas Day games for NFL football has not been matched with a sales executive who is versed in the nuances of such telecasts. “There’s an existing marketplace, and there’s an existing way of working, and a lot of these digital players think that they can just come in and sell, and it’s not that easy,” says one media buying executive with knowledge of the current market. Netflix declined to make executives available for comment. The streamer for years vowed never to sully its viewing experience with commercials, but media economics, and increased competition from services like Amazon’s Prime Video, HBO Max and Disney+ have not let it hold to those convictions. And just as Netflix has made a concentrated foray into ad sales, the market for streaming inventory has been undermined by a glut of supply. Amazon has loads of ads to sell, and traditional media outlets do as well. The sheer tonnage of streaming inventory available has given advertisers the upper hand in negotiations. To be sure, streaming is soaring. The volume of ad commitments put toward streaming in the most recent “upfront” video market rose a whopping 30%, according to consultancy Media Dynamics, hiking to about $17.2 billion, compared with about $13.2 billion in the 2025 market. But a rising swath of digital inventory, spurred by the rise of cheap FAST channels and increased inventory on mainstream streamers, has weakened the media companies’ stance. The cost of reaching 1,000 viewers, a key metric in these annual negotiations that is known as a CPM, is under clear pressure. Streaming CPMs during the upfront fell 4.9%, to $25.90 from $27.75, according to Media Dynamics. This upfront marked the third year in which media companies agreed to what is known as “rollbacks,” or reductions in the rate of change in pricing they seek for the viewers they deliver. “Free ad-supported TV channels are attracting accelerating audiences especially among increasingly challenged lower per capita income households,” says Pivotal Research Group analyst Jeff Wlodarczak in a recent research note. Other media companies are likely to face these pressures. Simply put, more streaming inventory is purchased via programmatic means, or via algorithms that seek out particular audience characteristics, such as expectant mothers or first-time car buyers. This digital automation of advertising inventory has made it harder for media companies to prove that such video opportunities are “premium,” or better than what else is available in the market. Some companies have tried to create new ways to stand out. Before its acquisition by Skydance, Warner Bros. Discovery burnished its ability to help advertisers identify specific settings and emotions present in its programming library. So a marketer might look for a scene set in an airport, grocery store or theme park, or seek out shows that made viewers feel a sense of mystery, curiosity or adrenaline. Paramount had touted a concept called a “streaming fixed unit” that gives advertisers who buy it the same ad placement in the premieres of new episodes of top shows such as “Tulsa King”. When an advertiser buys the unit, it is also buying a guarantee that Paramount will run the ad in a fixed place, such as the first spot in a commercial break, for the first seven days after the episode debuts. Netflix isn’t the first new-tech streaming purveyor to face challenges upon turning to the ad market. Amazon infamously pressed advertisers to pay more for “Thursday Night Football,” then untested as a stand-alone on the Prime Video platform, than they did for Fox’s Sunday-afternoon NFL games, some of the medium’s costliest properties. Media buyers pushed back , and Amazon is believed to have retreated from some of its highest price demands. To be sure, Netflix has something many advertisers want: Programing that gets attention. Blue chip marketers ranging from Coca-Cola to Anheuser-Busch and State Farm have turned logistical somersaults to link their products with programs like “Stranger Things,” “The Gentlemen” and “Running Point,” often with stand-out placements in and commercials liked to the series. The challenge, of course, is that the number of sponsorships available hinges on Netflix’ programming slate. “We’re still growing, our ads business is growing over 80% this year. And I think noting that if you are sufficiently aggressive with your product road map, you’re going to occasionally be behind some milestones,” Peters said, adding: “General demand remains very strong, the breadth of advertisers continues to expand, and ultimately, advertisers want our new products and features, and that’s a big mechanism of growth for us. So we are very focused on getting those out to them as quickly as we possibly can.” Getting more ad dollars into its funnel may require a little savvy. Buyers feel Netflix’ initial decision to focus on creating a stand-alone suite of ad-tech may have crimped some of its efforts. “They were trying to build their own walled garden, their own tech,” says the buying executive. “It is just going to slow down adoption, because you’re making it harder for us to work with you in the ways that we’re used to working.” Perhaps Netflix has heard this complaint. The company has struck deals in recent months to allow its programmatic ad inventory to be purchased via Amazon and Yahoo platforms. Last week, the company unveiled an expansion of its interaction with Trade Desk, a demand-side platform that functions as one of the bigger programmatic marketplaces. With sports the only programming format that truly lures the sizable and simultaneous crowds advertisers covet, Netflix may want to beef up its expertise. Too often, the buying executive notes, Netflix has been slow to reveal pricing terms or inventory packages it sought around sports properties. “There was confusion about even just basic things. Are you requiring a match spend on entertainment? When are you sending out plans? When are we negotiating pricing?” this buyer says. “They’re being too difficult to work with, and it just makes things harder.” Boosting ad sales may come as a distraction as Netflix executives fret about their service’s ability to keep subscribers and boost the number of hours they spend with the platform. Ted Sarandos , Netflix’s co-CEO, described a scenario under which Netflix had to work harder to develop relationships with producers, directors and other members of the creative community. A new executive, Peter Rice, formerly of Fox and Disney, has come aboard to focus on just that. The ad revenue will remain equally important, argues Dan Salmon, an analyst at New Street Research. “We expect mis-execution in the ad business to be added to the investors’ #1 concern about continued slumping engagement,” he says in a recent research note. title: Susan Saint James, ‘Name of the Game,’ ‘McMillan & Wife’ and ‘Kate & Allie’ Star, Dies at 80
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 7:11am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Susan Saint James Susan Saint James Susan Saint James, the Emmy-winning actress who delighted TV viewers with her light-hearted turns on The Name of the Game , McMillan & Wife and Kate & Allie before quitting at the peak of her powers, has died. She was 80. Saint James died Monday of pancreatic cancer, her family announced. Survivors include her third husband, Dick Ebersol, the former Saturday Night Live executive producer and head of NBC Sports whom she married in November 1981. The couple soldiered on after losing their youngest child, 14-year-old son Teddy, in a 2004 plane crash. Related Stories Movies Hubert de la Bouillerie, 'Woodstock' and 'Witches of Eastwick' Film Editor, Dies at 75 TV Alan Dysert, 'All My Children' Actor, Dies at 75 Saint James was someone who was “generous with her time and energy, which she valued more than money, and instinctively drawn to whoever needed lifting up,” her family said. “She taught her children to pause, be kind and look out for other people.” On the big screen, she went on the run with Peter Fonda in Outlaw Blues (1977); played the lustful target of Dracula in Love at First Bite (1979), starring George Hamilton; executed a heist with fellow suburbanites Jessica Lange and Jane Curtin in How to Beat the High Cost of Living (1980); and portrayed George Segal ’s wife in Carbon Copy (1981). A contract player at Universal, Saint James portrayed the frequently kidnapped editorial assistant Peggy Maxwell for three seasons (1968-71) on the stylish 90-minute NBC drama The Name of the Game . ( THR took a look back at the series in 2018). Peggy worked at Howard Publications for all three of the rotating characters on the “wheel” series — Tony Franciosa as hotshot reporter Jeff Dillon, Gene Barry as kingly publisher Glenn Howard and Robert Stack as FBI agent turned magazine editor Dan Farrell. Six months after The Name of the Game ’s final episode, Saint James was back on another 90-minute wheel series, McMillan & Wife , which began in rotation with Columbo and McCloud as part of the NBC Mystery Movie franchise. Like Peggy, Saint James’ Sally McMillan also got into trouble and helped solve crimes, here with her husband, San Francisco police commissioner Stewart “Mac” McMillan ( Rock Hudson ). She appeared on the show for five seasons through 1976, when she left in a contract dispute (Hudson stuck around the final sixth season). Saint James returned to series television in 1984 by reuniting with Curtin for the CBS sitcom Kate & Allie . On that show, two childhoods friends now divorced — Saint James’ free-spirited Kate McArdle and Curtin’s more by-the-books Allie Lowell — raise their kids (three in all) in a Greenwich Village brownstone they share. When Kate & Allie was canceled in 1989 after the sixth season — it was nominated three times for the Emmy for outstanding comedy series — Saint James decided to pretty much shut down her acting career. She told People magazine in 2002 that she was tired of being “one of those people juggling knives and melons and then [saying], ‘Toss me in a razor blade.’” Saint James received an Emmy in 1969 for her work in the first season of The Name of the Game , then added noms in 1970 and ’71. She also was nominated for McMillan & Wif e in 1972, ’73 and ’75 and for Kate & Allie in 1984 and ’85. Susan Saint James (right) and Jane Curtin on a 1984 episode of ‘Kate & Allie.’ Courtesy Everett Collection One of four kids, Susan Jane Miller was born in Los Angeles on Aug. 14, 1946. She and her family moved in 1958 to Rockford, Illinois, after her father, Charles, was named president of The Testor Corp., maker of tools and accessories for model kits, and the Hobby Industry Association of America. Her mother, Constance, was a schoolteacher. Saint James attended the Woodlands Academy of the Sacred Heart for high school and lived and modeled in France for about three years. Inspired by Paula Prentiss, she moved back to California to try acting when she was 20 — she lived at the Hollywood Studio Club — and quickly scored a part alongside Franciosa in the 1966 NBC/Universal TV movie Fame Is the Name of the Game . Directed by Stuart Rosenberg, who would soon helm Cool Hand Luke , it served as the pilot for The Name of the Game . Created by Jennings Lang, the series sported a budget of $400,000 an episode, the largest of its day (Universal’s Black Tower stood in for Howard Publications headquarters). It was canceled after its third season, during which the temperamental Franciosa was fired. In 1967, Saint James appeared in a failed pilot for a crime show called Ready and Willing that starred Jack Weston and Joe Flynn and in the George Peppard feature P.J. A year later, she showed up on the pilot episode of ABC’s It Takes a Thief , starring Robert Wagner, leading to a recurring role as the crook/love interest Charlene “Charlie” Brown. She also made three other films at Universal that were released in 1968: Jigsaw , starring Bradford Dillman ; What’s So Bad About Feeling Good? , starring Peppard and Mary Tyler Moore ; and the sequel Where Angels Go … Trouble Follows! , starring Rosalind Russell. When McMillan & Wife , created by Leonard Stern, bowed in September 1971, Saint James had just turned 25 while Hudson was closing in on 46. In a 1971 interview with Bobbie Wygant, Saint James described Sally McMillan, the daughter of a cop, as “Peggy Maxwell grown up.” “She’s still just as nutty and just as goofy, but she’s married to Rock Hudson, and they live a very sophisticated life, they have a very nice house,” she continued. “She can’t get anything done, she doesn’t do anything right, she gets him involved in all her terrible happenings. It’s kind of a comedy mystery.” Susan Saint James and Rock Hudson, stars of ‘McMillan & Wife.’ Courtesy Everett Collection At the start of the final season, Sally is killed in a plane crash with her and Mac’s never-seen son. Saint James moved to Connecticut in 1983 to star in Kate & Allie , which taped in New York City. The sitcom, created by Sherry Coben , debuted in March 1984 as a six-episode midseason replacement series but was quickly renewed for a full season in the fall. She and Curtin went head to head for outstanding lead actress in a comedy series at the Emmys in 1984 and ’85, with the former SNL star winning both times. As The New York Times wrote in 2007, “Jane Curtin’s Allie, the ex-wife of a cheating Connecticut doctor, is truly miserable, and so the better character.” When the sitcom ended after 122 episodes in March 1989, Saint James was 43 and would soon become pregnant with Teddy. She didn’t quit acting entirely, appearing on episodes of The Drew Carey Show , Law & Order: SVU , Suits and Upload and onstage in Connecticut in The Miracle Worker , but she focused on being an active volunteer with the Special Olympics and launching a business selling baby-gift baskets. Saint James, who had dated rocker Stephen Stills in the late ’70s, got together with Ebersol when she was about to host Saturday Night Live in October 1981. “She comes to New York, we met on a Sunday, I was in love with her by Monday, we were living together in a hotel by Tuesday, and she did the show on Saturday,” Ebersol said in a 2009 interview . “We were married six weeks later.” After she hosted, Ebersol took her out to dinner that night, and their photograph while kissing soon appeared in The New York Daily News with the headline, “When Dick Ebersol Books a Host, He Doesn’t Fool Around … On Second Thought, He Does.” When Kate & Allie became a hit, Ebersol left Saturday Night Live in April 1985 to raise the kids. On Nov. 28, 2004, a private plane carrying Ebersol and he and Saint James’ sons Charlie and Teddy crashed in snow and fog during an attempted takeoff from Montrose Regional Airport in Colorado (the Ebersoles owned a home in nearby Telluride). Charlie pulled his injured dad through a hole in the middle of the plane, but Teddy was killed — his body was discovered underneath the wreckage 24 hours later — as was the pilot and steward. Less than three weeks after the crash, Saint James recorded an interview with Tim Russert for the Today show to thank those who had reached out to her and her family. “If you know anybody that loses somebody, call them on the phone,” she said. “People always say, ‘I know you don’t want to be bothered.’ You can’t be bothered enough. It’s just fantastic, and I just want them to know that.” Her family on Tuesday called what she did in the immediate aftermath of Teddy’s death her “defining act … she delivered his eulogy as a note to each of her other children and her husband, giving them words to heal. Even in the deepest grief of her life, she put everyone else first.” In addition to her husband and Charlie, survivors include another son, William, whom she also had with Ebersol; her son and daughter, Harmony and Sunshine, whom she had with her second husband, makeup artist (and manager) Tom Lucas; her sister, Mercedes; a niece, actress Christa Miller ( Shrinking ); seven grandkids; and her beloved service dog, Lola. Her first husband was screenwriter Richard Neubert; they were married from 1967-68. “She never met a stranger,” her family noted. “Every person she met became the most important person in the room at that moment, from a fellow board member to the clerk at the shoe store, who usually walked away knowing her entire life story.” THR

title: The NFL’s Biggest Dramas This Season Are In the Broadcast Booth
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 7:07am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Troy Aikman is in the final year of his ESPN deal. Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images The NFL might be the undisputed king of TV content, but it is off-the-field drama that has dominated much of the conversation around the game this season so far. In particular, it was a widely reported altercation before the Los Angeles Rams-Buffalo Bills game at SoFi Stadium earlier this month … in the ESPN broadcast booth. To recap: ESPN’s lead play-by-play announcer Joe Buck signed a rich new contract with the company, but his longtime analyst partner Troy Aikman has not, resulting in reported bad blood between the boothmates. On-air, of course, viewers would have no clue (Buck and Aikman have continued to deliver a broadcast worthy of their decamillion dollar contracts), but the dispute has become fodder, and Aikman has not been willing to shy away from discussing it. The former Dallas Cowboys quarterback appeared on The Mike Fisher Show on Friday, where he was almost melancholy about what his future holds in media. “I never had any interest in going into television, it was just by happenstance that I even got into it,” Aikman said, recalling the outreach from Fox Sports . “I don’t know that if they hadn’t hired me, I would have gotten an opportunity anywhere else. And here I am, 25 years later, and now as I’m into my last year at ESPN, I’m realizing that this is something that could very well be taken away from me, and so for the first time, I’m realizing how much I really do, and I’ve always enjoyed it. “Until you risk having something taken away from you, I think sometimes you tend to maybe take things for granted,” he continued. “And so for the first time probably in my career, I’m realizing, you know, this is a great profession, it’s been a great ride for me, and I hope that it’s not over.” Joe Buck and Troy Aikman will also lead ESPN’s coverage of the Super Bowl this year. Julio Aguilar/Getty Images As the faces of Fox and ESPN’s NFL coverage, Aikman and Buck have been staples on Sundays (and more recently Mondays) for years. The looming end of that is ripping through sports, media and the league itself. And the situation comes as Disney is set to host its first Super Bowl since 2006, with Buck and Aikman set to lead the game from the booth (they have also been a big part of its marketing). But with their rich deals, nothing can be assured, and in the TV business, any opportunity to get a better deal or sign talent that could make a difference is typically taken fast. At a conference room in the InterContinental Barclay Hotel in Midtown Manhattan last week, NFL executive VP and chief media officer Hans Schroeder was asked about the Buck-Aikman-ESPN impasse. Schroeder, who is responsible for managing the league’s relationships with its media partners, said that it had “no concern” with the situation. “I don’t know if you watched the game on Monday night. It was an incredible game. An incredible game, and incredible coverage by Joe and Troy, just like they always do,” Schroeder told assembled journalists in the room, adding that the league was proud of Disney’s coverage, including its numerous altcasts with the Manning brothers, Pat McAfee and Star Wars , and with all the effort going into next year’s Super Bowl. “I think the fans are deserving of first-class game production, which Joe and Troy have — I think going back to ’02 or something was their first year — a history of doing that as well as anyone, and I think you’ll continue to see them do that as well as anyone.” Suffice it to say, it is not the story that the league or Disney want to be talking about right now. And yet, the ESPN broadcast booth drama underscores what has been perhaps the most tumultuous and uncertain year ever for NFL broadcasters. At CBS, Tony Romo’s preseason arrest for operating a vehicle while intoxicated (OWI) led to his eventual ouster from the network’s broadcast booth. His replacement, JJ Watt, was named the permanent successor last week when he was given a multiyear contract extension, with Skydance Sports chief David Berson praising him as “insightful, entertaining, passionate, meticulous in his preparation, and the ultimate teammate.” Greg Olsen is in the final year of his deal at Fox, and is looking for a new home, while current NFL names like Travis Kelce and Sean McVay have bubbled up as potential TV talent in chats with agents and network execs. A senior NFL source told THR that the league doesn’t micromanage the personnel decisions of its broadcast partners, and that it isn’t involved in the calls being made when it comes to talent. But that doesn’t mean the league doesn’t have any say. Sources at both the league and its rights partners paint the conversation around broadcasting as an ongoing conversation, with the league always interested in improving coverage of the game. More precisely, the league’s NFL deals require a quality of production from its partners that includes an A-team broadcast booth that can deliver a broadcast worthy of the league and its viewers (“first-class production,” as Schroeder said). It might be a mushy benchmark, but it does mean that more out there ideas like the Manningcast, the McAfeecase or animated altcasts remain secondary considerations, and that the main booth needs to have seasoned or otherwise A-list talent (like Tom Brady, who made his broadcast booth debut for Fox). The drama matters, because the NFL matters. While no real fans will turn off their NFL games because of some broadcast booth drama, the entire situation is a rare speed bump for what is otherwise the most reliable bet in all of TV. And yet: The broadcast booths may change, but there’s no reason to think that the NFL will ever become less relevant, or less watched. THR

title: ‘Every Contact Leaves a Trace’ Director on Why She Hired a Detective: ‘I’m Trying to Reconstruct a Life Story’
full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 7:03am PT ‘Every Contact Leaves a Trace’ Director on Why She Hired a Detective: ‘I’m Trying to Reconstruct a Life Story’ By Will Tizard Plus Icon Will Tizard Contributor @willtizard1 Latest ‘Third Land’ Director on the Risks of Chronicling the Lives of Iranian Refugees in Turkey: It Was ‘Extremely Tense and Frightening’ 2 hours ago Latvian Filmmaker Who Witnessed Last Days of the Soviet Union Portrayed in ‘Podnieks on Podnieks’ 12 months ago Albania’s Soviet-Tinged Propaganda Archives Reveal a Passion for the Cinematic, says Docmaker Roland Sejko 12 months ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "Every Contact Leaves a Trace" (Courtesy of Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival) U.S. artist and documentarian Lynne Sachs has often screened her past films at Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival , but she’s finally made it in person this year, serving on the First Lights jury, which evaluates docu debuts. Sachs says she’s been impressed by Ji.hlava films that span the globe while showcasing the full range of filmmaking approaches and perspectives. “There are about 24 movies to see. It’s kind of revelatory. Already I’ve seen two films here, one from Argentina and one from Congo and they really couldn’t be more different. They make you think about the documentary paradigm.” Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart A case in point, she says: “Positionality.” Whose perspective is an audience seeing and is the filmmaker’s role visible or even known? It’s something Sachs has made crystal clear in her newest film, “Every Contact Leaves a Trace,” screening at Ji.hlava in its Czech premiere. Sachs herself is clearly onscreen, investigating, making connections, doubting herself, and occasionally seeking help from a youthful niece and nephew as she goes through old business cards, some decades old, wondering at who gave them to her and what traces of lives contacting hers can still remain. The film is a kind of detective story that eventually enlists the actual analyses of forensic investigators as Sachs follows leads to track down people whose names remain in her box of hundreds of carefully preserved business cards – a good number she admits have lost all meaning to her. “I actually hired a detective at one point,” she confesses. Some left burning impressions on her and she has always wondered what became of the card giver – such as an artist whose work touched her years ago or a fellow artist filmmaker who was later canceled over allegations of impropriety. One card was from a Syrian woman whose family discouraged her from sitting for an on camera to share her experiences as a refugee – so Sachs settles for filming a tribute to the woman’s cooking skills. Sachs says she is also uneasy about terms that have come into common use for people in docus. Rather than say “protagonists” or “characters,” she much prefers “on camera participants.” Or maybe “visible collaborators who are the people in front of the camera.” “We’re offered the chance to tell our story by the person behind the camera. What I don’t know is, who is the person behind the camera?” In the case of “Every Contact,” it’s clear to all who is filming and inquiring as Sachs visibly, sometimes awkwardly, tracks down people who once met her but certainly never expected her to appear again at their doorstep with a camera. It’s a role she has not always put onscreen so clearly, she says. “I’m trying to reconstruct a life story of life experience from the interactions I’ve had with people…people who left a mark.” Since the film came out, Sachs says, people have offered her their own collections of old business cards. “I say, ‘Oh, no!’ This combination of cards only goes back to one person. You’re the person who had that dentist. You’re the person who met that psychoanalyst. Or potential friend on a bus.” As Sachs investigation progressed, she says, “I was most drawn to the cards that presented the biggest obstacles.” Some card donors may be impossible to find now. And others presented a different challenge: At times figures from your past have made lasting impressions – but that doesn’t always mean that was mutual. The process of recounting past encounters is one fraught with traps, says Sachs, as human minds tend to re-enact them in the mind, often editing, sometimes finding specific moments deeply burned in. As Sachs enlists the help of family on her quest, one suggests that it’s not usually even up to us to choose which memories will stay with us and which we’ll lose. Sachs discovered through her docu detective work that sometimes she did not need to fly across time zones to track down someone she once knew who might not even remember her or feel they shared an important interaction, she says. “I don’t need to prove I did or didn’t,” says Sachs. “I need to deal with the residue.” Jennifer Coolidge to Return for ‘The Watcher’ Season 2 ‘Decision to Leave’ Cinematographer Kim Ji-yong on Chasing Natural Light for Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’: ‘This Is the One Where We Worried, Debated and Planned the Most’ CAA’s Roeg Sutherland Says It’s Too Soon to Predict Fallout From Netflix Firings, Thinks Recent Mergers Represent ‘Opportunity’ for Industry Netflix Says 67% of Surveyed Members Want to Visit Korea as Busan’s Creative Asia Puts Locations in Focus How Netflix’s Messy Transition Will Rock Hollywood: Looking at You, NBCU ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ ‘Squid Game’ Stars Fete Netflix’s Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases ‘Tantara,’ ‘All of Us Are Dead’ Season 2 Loading comments...

title: Errol Morris Is Sitting on a Secret Elizabeth Holmes Interview (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Larry Busacca/Getty “I have this problem ,” shares Errol Morris , the Oscar-winning documentary filmmaker behind “The Thin Blue Line,” “The Fog of War” and countless other renowned docs. You see, the 78-year-old can’t seem to screen Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s docu-phenomenon on Elizabeth Holmes , “You Can See Everything.” He claims to have contacted the appropriate parties but has thus far been rebuffed. “Can you get me a screener?” he pleads. (I cannot.) Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart What Morris did do, however, was finally watch Alex Gibney’s 2019 documentary on Holmes and her sham blood-testing company Theranos — “The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley” — for the very first time. Morris, who’s directed “probably 1,000” commercials for various companies, was hired by Holmes in 2015 to shoot a series of ads for Theranos that depicted the “founder” staring wide-eyed into the camera that have attracted criticism for contributing to her mythmaking . Morris says he doesn’t know how Gibney got ahold of extra footage from the ads to use in “The Inventor,” but that’s not all: Morris exclusively revealed to Variety that he actually conducted a two-hour Interrotron interview with Holmes that he’s contemplating releasing in light of the renewed interest around the infamous grifter. So, I understand you have not seen “You Can See Everything,” but recently watched Alex Gibney’s documentary on Elizabeth Holmes, “The Inventor,” for the very first time. I never really wanted to see it until recently for a variety of different reasons, and I was quite surprised to find out that I was in it. He used outtakes from your Theranos ads, right? Well, what’s really not known about any of this is, yes, I did all the advertising for Theranos, but I did it at a time when Elizabeth Holmes was on the front cover of Forbes and many other magazines. She was riding high, and this was before everything collapsed. Did I have any reason to believe that she was a fraud? I did not. Did that change as time went on? It did. I had tried very hard, over a number of years, to do a documentary on Elizabeth Holmes and it would have happened except that she was under indictment. There was massive litigation going on. You wanted to interview Holmes for a documentary? I asked her, at a certain point, if I could film an interview with her — and this is at the height of her success — and I did film a two-hour interview with her, which is not very well-known if it is known at all. And I just watched that. I am sincerely interested in putting that out as an unedited film. You should. If anything, it gives you a comparison of Elizabeth before and Elizabeth after , which I think is interesting in and of itself. I noticed that the Gibney film begins and ends with my interview with Elizabeth Holmes. This two-hour interview you conducted with Holmes has not been seen by anyone other than yourself? Well, myself and the people in my office, but yes, for all intents and purposes, it has not been seen by anyone. Let me ask you a fast question: Why do you think [“ You Can See Everything ”] has proven so popular? I think it touches on a lot of different things that fascinate the culture — grifters, self-delusion to the point where the person created a persona that incorporated a fake Yoda voice, true crime and Silicon Valley megalomania channeled through the prism of Nathan Fielder’s brand of awkward comedy that pits, to borrow from John Ganz, a neurotic against a psychotic. Well, it’s hard for me to tell you about the film having not yet seen it, but I can tell you what I think about Elizabeth Holmes having spent a considerable amount of time with her. I was interviewed by John Carreyrou recently for an article that subsequently appeared in The New York Times, and he was questioning me about something I’d said to him many, many years ago when I was considering making a documentary about Elizabeth Holmes and had asked him if he would participate in that documentary. Some people see these stories as an on/off switch of she’s innocent or she’s guilty, she’s lying or she’s telling the truth. And when you’re investigating a crime, part of that investigation has to be if the person is guilty or innocent, since the criminal justice system works in such a way that you are looking for some kind of result. But what interests me is: To what extent was she self-deceived? To what extent did she believe in her own bullshit? Carreyrou understandably wants to tell you that she knowingly committed fraud, is guilty, should have been convicted and is in prison, as she should be. I keep wondering about the psychology of self-deception because part of me believes that she believes in Theranos and that she could achieve the results as promised. Aren’t there, say, serial killers who are convinced that what they’re doing is right and just? And isn’t it more about the people you hurt along the way? Yes, it is. You could say that lots of people in Silicon Valley misrepresent or out-and-out lie about what their technology can achieve, but in this case it involved medical results and people whose lives are directly affected by those medical results, and that in itself makes it different. One example of a lie would be that she’d claimed Theranos had a Department of Defense contract and its blood-testing technology was being deployed on the battlefield, none of which was true. Now, we can get into a philosophical discussion of the nature of lying and what is a lie, and did she lie in a very clear sense? Yes. Many, many times. Did she see them as lies? That is of interest to me. I want to ask you about something you’d said during a Reddit Q&A after Holmes’ house of cards collapsed: “When everything fell apart, I was shocked because I believed in Elizabeth Holmes. I feel, rightly or wrongly, that most of the television programs and movies about her have missed the mark. Did she do bad things? Most assuredly. The question remains, why?” You then drew a comparison between her and Joan of Arc. Probably the Robert Bresson “Joan of Arc,” which is one of my very favorite films. But Elizabeth Holmes wasn’t burned at the stake. She’s serving some time in prison for defrauding people. The nature of her punishment is not similar to being burned at the stake, and if you thought that’s what I meant by it, I did not. You were drawing that comparison in regard to their self-deception. One thing I can say about Joan of Arc: Do I think that God was speaking to her? I have a confession to make: I don’t believe in God. Do I think that God exists? No, I don’t! Do I think that God was directly communicating with Joan of Arc? I don’t! Do I think she thought that God was directly communicating with her? She did! She went to the stake on the basis of it. That’s your comparison. Going back to those Theranos promos you shot with her— —Don’t call them promos! I was hired as a commercial director, and I’ve shot probably 1,000 commercials. In the Gibney documentary, it is mentioned that Elizabeth Holmes and Patrick O’Neill, who was her CCO, had hired me because of the many Apple commercials I’d directed for Steve Jobs. If I had known how much of my interview was being used [by Gibney], or even if it was being used at all, I’m not sure what I would have said. I knew it was being used, but I never really wanted to watch [“The Inventor”]. Maybe I’d just had enough of it. How did Gibney get ahold of the footage? This I do not know. I really don’t know. And I’m not being coy or cagey. I do not know. I know the commercials you shot for Holmes and Theranos have garnered quite a bit of criticism for contributing to her mystique, but I found Holmes quite creepy in those commercials. How do you feel about people’s perception of those commercials? People have never seen my long interview that I did with Elizabeth Holmes. I’ve heard that I have been accused of representing a fraud — knowingly — and this is just not true. I’ll join a lot of other people who were on the Theranos board at the time that I was doing this series of commercials. Are you sure you want to join Henry Kissinger? I’m joking. I actually interviewed Henry Kissinger just before he died. Is that going to go anywhere? It might. I have so much stuff that I do nothing with. I’d heard a very funny story about how BP approached you to direct an ad for them following the Deepwater Horizon oil spill and that you proposed a wild idea that they turned down. I believe that’s true! And what was that idea? You tell me and I’ll tell you if it’s real! That Mel Gibson would be standing on a BP oil platform and say something to the effect of, “If anyone knows about a public relations disaster, it’s me.” That’s it! And of course, they said no. Fortunately, enough people have said yes over the years, but I can’t tell you how many people have said no. I once said to my producer for commercials, “You know, I get all these commercials, but I’ve never gotten diarrhea or erectile dysfunction commercials. What’s wrong with me?” I once got a Depend commercial, and my ideas for incontinence/Depend commercials were by and large rejected. What was one of those ideas that you really liked? Thank you for asking. I had just done a long interview with Janis Karpinski, who’d just been demoted in connection with Abu Ghraib — and this interview has never seen the light of day — so there’s this lady general inside a tank in a war zone. Shells are exploding all around. The tank is on maneuvers. We see the face of the lady general inside the tank. She has an enormously pinched expression. She is fidgety, edgy. And then, you hear the sound of running water, and the expression on her face changes to one of total relaxation and pleasure. And then we cut outside and we see the artillery exploding. Depend . That is hilarious. The guy who was producing the commercials to Depend put his face two inches away from mine and said, “THERE IS NOTHING, NOTHING FUNNY ABOUT INCONTINENCE!” And I said, “I guess I beg to differ.” I’m with you on that one. By the way, why did your two-hour Elizabeth Holmes interview never come out? Because the company fell apart and she was prosecuted… but I can’t really answer it. The clearest answer is that I’d moved on. But now I feel pretty strongly that this is an interesting document — not because I’m trying to prove something about Elizabeth Holmes, but it does provide some kind of evidence of what she was like when everything was going her way. And what is your takeaway after watching the interview? That she was a true believer. Loading comments... title: Susan Saint James Dies: ‘McMillan & Wife’, ‘Kate & Allie’ Actor Was 80
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Billy Crystal’s ‘860’ Extends Broadway Run To February Sylvester Stallone On Casting Daughter In ‘Tulsa King’: “Of Course It’s Nepotism, You Idiot” Ric Flair Latest Health Update: Ex-Wrestler Wears Eye Patch In Message Reassuring Fans “I Am Focused On My Healing And Recovery” View All October 27, 2026 6:56am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Susan Saint James in 1974 Albert Watson / TV Guide / Everett Collection Susan Saint James , the husky-voiced actress who starred in such popular TV series as McMillan & Wife and Kate & Allie, died Monday, October 26, of pancreatic cancer. She was 80. A rep for Saint James confirmed her death to People. Among her survivors are husband Dick Ebersol, the former President of NBC Sports and executive producer of NBC’s Saturday Night Live. Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries Obituaries Walter Koenig Dies: ‘Star Trek’s Original Ensign Chekov Was 90 In a statement, Saint James’ family described her as “generous with her time and energy, which she valued more than money, and instinctively drawn to whoever needed lifting up. She taught her children to pause, be kind and look out for other people.” “She never met a stranger,” the family statement continues. “Every person she met became the most important person in the room at that moment, from a fellow board member to the clerk at the shoe store, who usually walked away knowing her entire life story. Her defining act: weeks after losing her youngest son, Teddy, in the November 28, 2004 plane crash, she delivered his eulogy as a note to each of her other children and her husband, giving them words to heal. Even in the deepest grief of her life, she put everyone else first. Days after the crash she sat with Tim Russert to thank the people who had reached out and to tell them the family was okay.” The statement concluded, “She brought that same fire and positivity to everything that followed, and never lost it. She is survived by her husband, Dick Ebersol, her four children–Sunshine Lucas, Harmony Lucas, Charlie Ebersol and Willie Ebersol–her seven grandchildren; her sister, Mary Mercedes Dewey, as well as her beloved service dog, Lola.” Born Susan Jane Miller on August 14, 1946, in Los Angeles, Saint James was raised in Rockford, Illinois, where she began modeling as a teen. She launched her acting career in a 1966 TV movie called Fame Is the Name of the Game, then booked guest roles in the series Ironside and, when the TV movie became a series titled The Name of the Game , Saint James landed a series regular role. In 1968, she had a co-starring role in Where Angels Go, Trouble Follows , the sequel to the popular comedy The Trouble with Angels. Susan Saint James, Rock Hudson, ‘McMillan & Wife’ (1973) Albert Mackenzie Watson/ TV Guide /ABC/Everett Collection Other TV episodic work from the era included roles in It Takes a Thief and Alias Smith and Jones, but her early signature role arrived in 1971 when she was cast opposite Rock Hudson in the light crime drama series McMillan & Wife , a highly popular program that had Saint James portraying the younger wife and partner in crime-solving. The show lasted for six seasons, with its finale on April 24, 1977, but Saint James had departed early over a contract dispute. Her character was killed off in a plane crash and the “& Wife” part of the title was erased. The show didn’t survive another season; by the end of her run, Saint James had received four Emmy nominations for her performance. Saint James remained a prolific actor following her departure from the successful series, co-starring with Peter Fonda in the film Outlaw Blues (1977), George Hamilton in Love At First Bite (1979), and Jessica Lange and Jane Curtin in How To Beat The High Cost of Living (1980). Jane Curtin, Susan Saint James, ‘Kate & Allie’ (1984) Mario Casilli/TV Guide/CBS/Everett Collection Saint James and Curtin would reunite four years later in what would become high career points for both stars: The CBS sitcom Kate & Allie premiered on March 19, 1984, with the two stars portraying divorced mothers (and childhood friends) with children who decide to share a home in New York’s Greenwich Village. Saint James portrayed Kate, the more free-spirited of the two, with Curtin as the higher-strung conservative Allie. The combination proved a winner (and would be echoed decades later in the Jane Fonda-Lily Tomlin comedy Grace and Frankie ), and the series, created by Sherry Coben, was a hit with critics and audiences, appreciated for its intelligent humor and warm, groundbreaking, chosen-family approach. Saint James was nominated for two Emmys for her performance as Kate, with Curtin nominated for three and winning two. Following Kate & Allie, Saint James largely retired from show business – she’d appear in guest roles periodically – devoting her time to raising a family that included two children from her second marriage, to make-up artist Thomas Lucas, and the three sons she had with third husband, the Saturday Night Live executive producer Dick Ebersol. (She and Ebersol met when she guest-hosted the NBC comedy in 1981). Tragedy struck on November 28, 2004, when a private plane carrying Ebersol and sons Charles and Teddy crashed at the Montrose Regional Airport in Colorado. Dick and Charles Ebersol survived, but 14-year-old Teddy was killed (along with a pilot and flight attendant). After her son’s death, Saint James often devoted her time working with parents who had lost children. Saint James is survived by Ebersol, four children, seven grandchildren, and sister Mary Mercedes Dewey. title: Matthew Perry Netflix Docuseries: Five Takeaways From Flimsy Look At ‘Friends’ Star’s Life & Death
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Jay Z & Apple Make It Official! Hova’s Headlining The Super Bowl Halftime Show Neil Young Rocks Trump With $10M Suit Over Using That ‘Free World’ Tune Again ‘Smear’ Campaign: George Clooney, Betty Gilpin, Adam Scott & Laverne Cox Team To Read Clark Gregg-Penned Political Play As Midterms Fundraiser View All October 27, 2026 6:48am Add us as a Google Preferred Source (L-R) Roger Castillo, Matthew Perry, & David Pressman in The One About Matthew Perry Netflix SPOILER ALERT: The following article contains details about Netflix ‘s The One About Matthew Perry docuseries. Let’s be honest, Netflix’s just debuted The One About Matthew Perry is mainly for the hardcore Friends fans. Having said that even the devotees of Rachel, Ross, Monica, Joey, Phoebe and Chandler might be disappointed as there’s not much in this Mary Robertson directed three-part docuseries you haven’t heard before. Related Stories News Remembering Matthew Perry: A TV & Film Career In Photos Legal Matthew Perry Death: “Ketamine Queen” Sentenced For ‘Friends’ Star’s 2023 Overdose Over the approximately three-hour running time, The One About draws on tales of drunken nights, funny faces, and the rise, demands, and bends of fame. There’s interviews with old friends, family members (especially Perry’s younger half-sister and licensed therapist Mia Perry Bowick), NBC Entertainment boss Warren Littlefield, The Whole Nine Yards director and one now ex-U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California. Still, in a rush to get not really anywhere at all, the result is pretty much the officially authorized surface level stuff we all used to get in the 1990s from Behind the Music . Unlike VH1’s sometimes under appreciated Behind the Music, The One About Matthew Perry ‘s three-act play of the rise, the fall, and the resurrection never really gains much momentum. The comeback of sorts the third act should promise leaves you feeling at best deceived. The primary fuel here is the people who love the long time addiction-addled Perry, who drowned at the age of 54 in his West L.A. hot tub on October 28, 2023 after taking a ton of ketamine, clearly loved him a lot, and miss him a lot. Yet, The One About ( Friends fans get the nod to the successful sitcom) mainly leans on Perry’s best-selling 2022 Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing memoir and its subsequent press tour for its narrative. A decision that, as we know now in hindsight of the book itself, reveals little of the darkness-plagued man behind the Friend, if you know what I mean? Watch on Deadline Still, for better and worse, here are some of the highlights of The One About Matthew Perry : (L-R) Lisa Kudrow , Matt Leblanc , Courteney Cox , David Schwimmer , Jennifer Aniston , Matthew Perry, THERE ARE NO FRIENDS: if you are expecting to hear from Jennifer Aniston, Courteney Cox, Matt LeBlanc, Lisa Kudrow or David Schwimmer in The One About Matthew Perry, you are going to be very upset. While the Friends cast are seen thoughout The One About in behind the scenes footage, clips from the 10-season show, and on press junkets, none of them acquiesced to be interviewed by Robertson. In fact no one from Friends , not the cast, not guest stars, not co-creators Marta Kauffman and David Crane appear in the docuseries. The closest The One About ever gets to the mega-sitcom is one Jeff Strauss, who was a writer/producer on Season 1 of Friends. While Strauss appears to have been close to Perry initially as Friends came together, most of his subsequent observations and remarks about the actor becoming “challenging and problematic” are clearly second-hand at best. MATTHEW PERRY REALLY WANTED TO BE FAMOUS & THEN REALLY HATED BEING FAMOUS: The son of a journeyman actor and an ex-press secretary to a Canadian PM, Perry was also the stepson of a famous Canadian journalist and later Dateline NBC correspondent. From early days as the class clown to hanging around sets with his father figures and trying to catch a break in early 1990s L.A., Perry, as various pre-fame pals attest in docuseries, wanted to be famous. When he got there with Friends , on a level barely anyone achieves nowadays, it was overwhelming. To be precise as one can on such occasions, it seems to, from the docuseries and Perry’s own memoir, brought out crippling insecurities, as much as wealth and notoriety. Problem with The One About , unlike Robertson’s much better last Netflix docuseries Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV, is that it is mostly examined though the lens of the spiraling booze, drug and emotional problems with little sense of context — which feels as hollow as canned studio audience laughter. Also, with that Little Richard attributed quote of “if you don’t want your picture taken, don’t become famous” in mind, the openly ambitious Perry himself is rarely held responsible for his own behavior, actions and addiction. It seems from The One About Matthew Perry that Matthew Perry was a ultimately a perpetual victim who, to quote one of his buddies from the series, “didn’t stand much of a chance” — and that’s just hard to buy. THERE WAS MORE THAN JUST FRIENDS : The stardom and sprawling legacy of Friends, even though it ended nearly 20 years before Perry’s death, seems to have haunted him in both a Hollywood cliche way and a very real disorienting way until the day he died. Spending decades outrunning Chandler Bing, Perry may have never given himself the ability to let go and find success elsewhere, The One About suggests While praised for short and Emmy-nominated stints on The West Wing, Ally McBeal, and The Good Wife , Perry may have floundered on the big screen but his TV leading roles from 2006 – 2013 displayed untapped talents that never got the time or space to thrive. Looking back from the streaming and revival standpoint of 2026, Perry’s leading roles on Aaron Sorkin’s flawed but prophetic Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip , Mr. Sunshine (which Perry co-created) and Go On all deserve much more attention, Robertson postulates in the second episode of The One About . There’s not a lot to argue with the Emmy winner’s POV on that — if only Robertson had done those later shows and roles justice. Getty THE ONE ABOUT DOESN’T HAVE A LOT ABOUT PERRY’S DEATH: I was at court hearings and sentencing hearing on Perry’s death right up until this year. Before that, I was on the story of Perry’s death within an hour or so of his body being discovered in late October 2023 by authorities in his Pacific Palisades home. As more details came out, the sad truth of Perry’s relapses and drug hustle emerged. What also emerged was the fast one the actor played on those around him — pronouncing himself clean and sober when he kept going back to using made his death look inevitable. Like the cast of Friends, you won’t find a lot of that in The One About Mathew Perry – it doesn’t fit the narrative they’ve constructed, true or not. One can debate the truth and consequence of Perry’s life and death for ages, I grant you as someone who saw a lot of it unfold close up. Yet, playing primarily on the slop side of the Netflix street, the docuseries doesn’t give you much more time than to take a breath before the epilogue begins. The One About gives Perry’s death, the investigation and convictions of the scummy doctors, personal assistant and the infamous “Ketamine Queen ” just around 15 minutes at the end of the third and final episode. In a summary, bad people did some bad things. While that is partially true, you never learn anything more nuanced about it than that — which makes the almost three hours up to that point feel like a psych-out of the viewer and the subjects in the docuseries. THIS IS WHY PEOPLE SPEND LESS TIME ON NETFLIX: Love it, hate or just eat it, few nowadays are going to tell you fast food is nutritious. Besides a few funny clips from old Friends episodes and some of Perry’s later work, there is nothing good for you or really even memorable about The One About Matthew Perry once you’ve watched all the episodes. In many ways, the whole series is a juiced up version of Netflix’s recently introduced InstaDocs series and their insta-take on a large event like the OpenAI Hugging Face cyberattack. In another sense, The One About Matthew Perry seems to exist in no small measure to get the streamer’s algorithm to pump you over to more easily digestible programming that you’ll lose interest in fairly quickly. As a passionate fan of Is It Cake? , don’t expect me to regal you with highbrow or die recommendations. Good escapism is a treat to me, and a tasty one at that the better it is cooked. However, at the same time, if you want to know, Ted and Greg, why Netflix subscribers are spending less time on the service, it is air-filled content like The One About Matthew Perry . Content that is truly much ado about nothing. The limited-engagement production, which opened to favorable reviews on October 21, was originally set to close Sunday, January 3, 2027, but has been extended due to popular demand. title: ‘Babel’: THR’s 2006 Review
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ray Bennett Plus Icon Ray Bennett View All October 27, 2026 6:16am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Brad Pitt in 2006's 'Babel.' Everett On Oct. 27, 2006, Paramount unveiled Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Babel in theaters following its premiere in competition at the Cannes Film Festival in May. The feature, starring Brad Pitt, Cate Blanchett and Gael Garcia Bernal, was nominated for seven Oscars at the 79th Academy Awards, including best picture. It walked away with one win, in the original score category. The Hollywood Reporter’s original review is below: Tense, relentless and difficult to watch at times, Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Babel is an emotionally shattering drama in which a simple act of kindness leads to events that pierce our veneer of civilization and bring on the white noise of terror. Iñárritu and screen writer Guillermo Arriaga involve six families, most of them not known to one another, in four countries on three continents in their story of random fate and the perils of being unable to communicate. Brad Pitt, Cate Blanchett and Gael Garcia Bernal give committed ensemble performances alongside seasoned character performers and nonactors as the story ranges from Morocco to San Diego to Tokyo. The film, which also features exceptional work by director of photography Rodrigo Prieto, production designer Brigitte Broch, editors Stephen Mirrione and Douglas Crise and composer Gustavo Santaolalla, is headed for major prizes and large, appreciative audiences. As with his previous films, Iñárritu tells his story using scenes out of order so that the pieces fall together in a jagged form that heightens the tension. It starts in the Moroccan desert, where a man buys a Winchester rifle from a neighbor to help keep the jackals away from his herd of goats. A Japanese hunter had gifted the neighbor with the rifle in gratitude for his work as a guide. The rifle is entrusted to the goat herder’s two young sons, who end up firing it from a mountainside at a coach filled with Western tourists just to see how far the bullet would go. The bullet, however, strikes an American named Susan (Blanchett) who is traveling with her husband Richard (Pitt) in attempt to patch up their marriage following the death of a child. Four hours from the nearest hospital, the coach takes a detour to a remote village, where a local man offers shelter while the other tourists argue over whether to stay or leave. Desperate, Richard phones the U.S. embassy pleading for help and also calls home in San Diego, where their longtime maid Amelia (Adriana Barraza) is caring for their other two children. With Susan bleeding and near death in the desert, he begs Amelia to remain with the kids as he tries to get help. Amelia’s son, however, is getting married across the border and, having exhausted attempts to find another sitter, she decides to take the kids with her to the wedding in a car driven by her friendly but hot headed nephew Santiago (Bernal). As Richard fights to keep Susan alive with the help of a wise and calm old Moroccan woman and a veterinarian, the shooting escalates into an international incident with security forces believing terrorists to be responsible and hunting for the perpetrators. Meanwhile, in Tokyo, a young deaf-mute woman named Chieko (Rinko Kikuchi) is grappling with the loss of her mother by suicide, fighting with her equally bereft father (Koji Yakusho) and trying to deal with the frustrations of adolescence. The filmmakers succeed brilliantly in weaving these stories together, taking time to explore depth of character and relationships. The suspense builds throughout as everyone involved becomes lost in a place they don’t understand with people they don’t know if they can trust. Several astonishing Tokyo sequences replicate what it might be like to be deaf-mute, and equal imagination is applied to scenes at night in the wasteland of the Mexico-California border and the barren mountains of Morocco. — Ray Bennett, originally published on May 24, 2006. THR

title: ‘Derek Vs Derek’: British Rewilding Doc About Warring Neighbors Tests Its “Unexpected” Protagonists In All The Right Ways
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max BAFTA Names New Chair Stephen & Simon Cornwell Take On Chairmen Roles At ‘Night Manager’ Producer The Ink Factory As Michele Wolkoff Upped To President Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK View All October 27, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Derek vs Derek' Joss Barratt Welcome to Global Breakouts , Deadline’s strand in which, each fortnight, we shine a spotlight on the TV shows and films killing it in their local territories. The industry is as globalized as it’s ever been, but breakout hits are appearing in pockets of the world all the time and it can be hard to keep track… So, we’re going to do the hard work for you. We’re in the UK this week spotlighting an environmental documentary about warring neighbors that is gaining big traction. With a U.S. premiere coming shortly, Derek vs Derek has taken years to get to the big screen. Its exec producer Adam Wishart sets out its journey below. Related Stories News The "Algorithm Breaking" 'Hunkkaar' Has Challenged Indian Audiences On The Limits Of Procedural TV - And Their Own Beliefs News International Insider: The Final Edinburgh... Or Is It?; Int'l Oscar Race Begins Name: Derek vs Derek Country: UK Producer: The Slate Works & Damer Films Distributor: CAT&Docs For fans of: Wilding Watch on Deadline Many years in the making, Derek vs Derek started life as a story of rewilding and arrived in cinemas as something quite different, a “universal” tale of warring neighbors who nevertheless never stop learning from each other, says the film’s exec producer, Adam Wishart. The low-budget British documentary is riding on a high and is about to screen in the U.S. for the first time, but its journey to the big screen has been long and winding. The movie follows two neighboring farmers in Devon, enjoyably both called Derek, one of whom, Derek Gow, is a rewilding conservationist, and the other, Derek Banbury, an intensive dairy farmer. Both have a natural distrust of their namesake, but are just about willing to hear them out. Wishart, a BAFTA nominee for the BBC and Apple TV’s fantastic 9/11: Inside the President’s War Room, lives in Devon, a short journey from Gow’s farm. He became aware of Gow and his work some time ago when he was advising on community regeneration. Derek Gow Joss Barratt Wishart was told a director, James Dawson, had been following Gow for some years in order to make a rewilding documentary similar to 2023 hit Wilding . He “tried to get the film commissioned and even used every piece of TV industry capital I had,” but Wishart kept running into brick walls. He felt something was missing. “I was supportive [of Dawson’s vision], but a little sceptical,” says Wishart. “Then he told me that, whenever he stayed with Derek Gow, Derek would point him towards the Banburys and tell him to go and have breakfast with them. Suddenly, it became apparent that there was a lovely film about their relationship and their two different visions.” Wishart knew this was more than a kernel of an idea and Dawson already had plenty footage, but funding was tricky to come by. In the end, money flowed in via a grant from the Redford Center foundation plus crowdfunding. “We’ve made it with a tiny budget, drawing favors from across the industry, with the whole endeavour held together by sticky back plastic and paperclips,” says Wishart, whose production house The Slate Works produced Derek vs Derek alongside Damer Films, with CAT&Docs handling international sales. While “getting documentaries off the ground has always been difficult,” Wishart notes that “it’s harder than ever to do something that doesn’t have an obvious hook – an anniversary, a major event or a famous celebrity.” Testing the protagonist Derek Banbury Joss Barratt The doc sees the Dereks execute their opposing visions while going about their day-to-day lives. Gow is a rewilder who is taking drastic measures like introducing wild boars to his farmland, and he wants to go even further by convincing locals to allow wolves to return to the UK. Banbury is a traditional farmer who is really about making ends meet. Slowly, and at times with great drama, their outlooks move closer towards each other, and Derek vs Derek by no means takes sides. Wishart feels the key to the doc’s success is really in the protagonists’ relationship and their individual characters, which he describes as “brilliant and rather archetypal, but also unexpected.” “There aren’t many documentaries about people like them,” he adds. “We live in such a polarized world that we assume two people with opposing views are going to fall out over every aspect of their lives and never speak again. But it’s perfectly possible to disagree about one aspect of your life and still call your neighbor if your tractor gets stuck.” Speaking a few weeks after the launch of Tom Cruise-starring satirical polemic Digger, Wishart feels docs and features about this subject matter have become overly preachy. “They make one group of people feel that their life choices are wonderful, while alienating another group,” he adds. “I thought [ Derek vs Derek ] was interesting because making a film that sits with only one protagonist can be problematic. It can feel like an ‘NGO film’ or piece of advocacy without much edge. The protagonist isn’t really being tested.” Gow and Banbury are now pals, and Wishart speaks to them frequently, with the pair appearing on Q&A panels around the country to support the movie. Wishart says the movie has made around £120,000 ($160,000) so far. According to the BFI, ticket sales for Derek vs Derek rose 114% week-on-week after launch. The movie has aired at festivals including in Thessaloniki and Zurich and will soon be given its U.S. premiere at New York’s Doc NY. While Wishart is “not betting my mortgage on it,” he says “if the film can find a wider audience” by perhaps picking up U.S. distribution, thereby “beginning conversations about how we relate to the natural world and the food system, then more power to it.” That, he thinks, is the beauty of Derek vs Derek, a “universal” story of grumpy neighbors that could maybe, whisper it, teach audiences a thing or two without them even realizing it. title: David Bowie Returns to Berlin With Immersive Event
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 5:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source David Bowie JTE Photo ©Blackout David Bowie is coming back to Berlin. Oscar-nominated documentary filmmaker Brett Morgen ( Moonage Daydream , On the Ropes ) will present the world premiere of Stage , his new immersive David Bowie concert experience, at the 2027 Berlinale . Morgen designed the immersive concert around original camera footage from Bowie’s 1978 Isolar II World Tour, which the director discovered while doing research for his 2022 documentary on Bowie, Moonage Daydream . The tour features Bowie performing material from Heroes , the landmark album he wrote and recorded while living in Berlin. Like Moonage Daydream , Stages was created with the cooperation of the David Bowie Estate. Bowie, a genre- and gender-bending icon of pop music , and one of biggest rock stars in history, died in 2016 , aged 69. Related Stories TV HBO's 'Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone' Casts James and Lily Potter, Charlie Weasley Business Hilary Rosen Named BAFTA Chair Stages features a three-screen presentation combining large-scale projections of the recovered and restored footage alongside transparent LED screens and a lighting design from Patrick Woodroffe, who has lit and designed tours for everyone from ABBA and The Police to Adele and Michael Jackson. He also lit Martin Scorsese’s Rolling Stones’ concert documentary Shine a Light , which opened the Berlinale in 2006. Paul Massey, the Academy Award-winning sound mixer of Bohemian Rhapsody (and 11-time Oscar nominee), created a special sound mix for Stages to give the audience the experience of being at the center of a live David Bowie concernt. Stages will have its world premiere at Berlin’s Uber Arena on Feb. 14, on the first weekend of the Berlinale. Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle called the event “a dream come true” for the festival. “The Berlinale is a place where cinema, art, and new forms of storytelling intersect,” she said. “To have this world premiere [of Stages ] in Berlin, a city so closely connected to David Bowie, makes the experience especially meaningful.” Morgen was Oscar-nominated for his 1999 boxing documentary On The Ropes and has directed several acclaimed docs, including Cobain: Montage of Heck (2015), on Kurt Cobain, the Emmy-winning Jane (2017) on the primatologist Jane Goodall, and The Kid Stays in the Picture (2002), on legendary Paramount producer Robert Evans. Morgen will attend the Berlinale and be a headline contributor to the European Film Market’s talks program. The 77 th Berlin International Film Festival runs Feb. 10-21, 2027. THR
