title: Brett Morgen’s David Bowie Immersive Concert Experience Set For Berlinale World Premiere
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Vantage Media Takes North American Rights To Pole-Dancing Drama ‘Exotic’ As Trailer Unveiled Brett Morgen’s David Bowie Immersive Concert Experience Set For Berlinale World Premiere Horror ‘The Block’ With Jack Falahee, Saphira Moran & Jackie Earle Haley Wraps; Unveils First Look View All October 27, 2026 4:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source David Bowie “Stage” Blackout The spirit of late pop and rock icon David Bowie is set to return to Berlin , the city he called home in the mid-1970s. The Berlin Film Festival has announced it will world premiere U.S. documentarian Brett Morgen ’s immersive concert experience David Bowie “Stage ” during its 77th edition in the city’s 17,000-capacity Uber Arena venue. Combining previously unseen Bowie concert footage and an immersive sound and light experience, the production is billed as “a new way of experiencing one of the most influential artists of the 20th century”. Related Stories News Berlinale 2027 Retrospective To Explore Visions Of The Future In Nod To Centenary Of Fritz Lang's 'Metropolis' News Quiver Distribution Takes U.S. For Jérémy Comte's Ghana & Canada-Set Drama 'Paradise' The work is designed around recently discovered and restored footage from the 1978 Isolar II World Tour, during which Bowie performed material from his landmark album ‘Heroes.’ Watch on Deadline Morgen first discovered the original camera negatives while working on his Grammy Award-winning, Oscar-nominated bio-doc Moonage Daydream, charting Bowie’s life and career. World premiering in Cannes in 2022, it was the first film to be officially authorized by Bowie’s estate. The new three-screen immersive experience combines large-scale projections and transparent LED screens with an elaborate lighting design by lighting designer Patrick Woodroffe, whose credits include collaborations with The Rolling Stones and Elton John. The production is further enhanced by a specially created sound mix from Academy Award winner Paul Massey ( Bohemian Rhapsody , Michael, Moonage Daydream ), and places audiences at the centre of a live concert experience using state-of-the-art 7.1 surround technology and spatial audio design. The production is a collaboration between Rob Hallett’s Wonderworld, the David Bowie Estate and Morgen. “David Bowie has bestowed upon us an extraordinary treasure, an unprecedented concert experience that has yet to be witnessed,” said live entertainment veteran and former AEG International President Hallet. “Working hand-in-hand with David Bowie’s Estate and Brett Morgen, we are ensuring this experience is 100% faithful to his legacy while making his genius accessible to global fans and a new generation.” Berlinale Director Tricia Tuttle added: “To have this world premiere in Berlin, a city so closely connected to David Bowie, makes the experience especially meaningful,” added Tricia Tuttle, Director of the Berlinale. “The Berlinale is a place where cinema, art, and new forms of storytelling intersect. It’s like a dream come true: Bowie, Brett Morgen, a world-class sound and light team all coming together in the city’s premiere music arena.” Morgen, whose credits also include Kurt Cobain bio-doc Cobain: Montage of Heck and Jane about Jane Goodall, will also be a headline speaker in the talks program of the Berlinale’s European Film Market (EFM). The 77th Berlinale will run from February 10 to 21, 2027, with the David Bowie “Stage ” world premiering on February 14. title: Hilary Rosen Named BAFTA Chair
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 2:58am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Hilary Rosen Courtesy of BAFTA Hilary Rosen has been promoted to BAFTA chair, succeeding Sara Putt. Putt steps down after a three-year term, with her deputy stepping up to fill the role. Rosen will oversee BAFTA’s mission to champion film, games and television talent through its awards, industry leadership and year-round development programs. A BAFTA Television Committee member since 2021 and later its chair, Rosen helped shape the TV and Craft Awards and oversee their juries, according to the British film and TV academy. Outside of BAFTA, Rosen is director of commissioning at UKTV, leading its slate of original scripted and unscripted content. She’ll be supported by Ade Rawcliffe and Andrew Miller as deputy chairs of the Academy. They’ll both serve a two-year term. And after a thorough election process, the following have been appointed to the Board of Trustees: Charu Desodt and Caroline Levy are the new Chairs for BAFTA’s Games and Television Committees, while Nahrein Kemp will take up the role of LIT Committee Chair. Shrina Shah, chair of the governance and appointments committee, will join the BAFTA Board of Trustees. Rosen described the promotion as “a great privilege.” She continued: “I have long been passionate about everything BAFTA does to promote the screen arts and champion talent across the screen industries… I am delighted to be able to do this alongside our newly appointed committee chairs, Charu, Caroline and Nahrein and the rest of the BAFTA Board of Trustees. All are outstanding industry leaders, and with the collective passion and insight we share, I’m confident that this Board of Trustees will continue to build on the important and impactful work that has gone before.” THR

title: ‘The One About Matthew Perry’ Review: Netflix’s Intimate and Sincere but Overly Padded Docuseries
full_text: × Skip to main content By Daniel Fienberg Plus Icon Daniel Fienberg Chief Television Critic TheFienPrint Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 12:01am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Matthew Perry and Mia Perry Bowick. Netflix Logo text Perhaps it’s most helpful to begin a discussion of Netflix ‘s three-part The One About Matthew Perry with an acknowledgment of the things that it is not. Directed by Mary Robertson ( Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV ), The One About Matthew Perry is not a salacious documentary about Perry’s death and the subsequent criminal investigations. Peacock already did one of those, and if you skipped it, you’re better off. The One About Matthew Perry The Bottom Line A fine feature-length doc unnecessarily extended into a three-hour docuseries. Airdate: Tuesday, October 27 (Netflix) Director: Mary Robertson The One About Matthew Perry also isn’t a definitive celebration of the life and comic genius of Matthew Perry, as related by those who worked with him most closely. Related Stories Business Netflix Hires Former Apple Exec Steve Wilson to Lead Podcast Acquisitions Business Ted Sarandos Swoops Into Seoul as Netflix Celebrates 10 Years in Korea That is to say, it’s not a documentary designed to spawn “10 Fun Things We Learned From…” listicles and — despite the pandering title, with its borrowing of Friends episodic nomenclature — it’s only a documentary about Matthew Perry and his hit NBC sitcom insofar as you can’t tell Perry’s story without reciting nostalgic talking points about Friends . Even if it might be better if you could. Literally none of Perry’s Friends co-stars appear in the documentary — nope, not even Janice or Gunther — nor do any of the key creative forces from the show. Unless you count Warren Littlefield, NBC’s entertainment president at the time, as a creative force from the show. Otherwise, one writer from the first season (Jeff Strauss) is included, but nobody with a high enough profile is there to say anything that might be interpreted as sensational or sensationalistic. The same is roughly true of the rest of the A-listers whom Perry worked with over the years. Fools Rush In is represented by producer Doug Draizin, Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip (and Mr. Sunshine ) by Nate Torrence, The Whole Nine Yards by director Jonathan Lynn. I can’t say whether or not Robertson reached out to the various big names in Perry’s celebrity sphere, but it’s my instinct both that she did not and that none of them would have agreed to participate anyway. The bigger the names you get, the more the focus of the documentary becomes what Lisa Kudrow or David Schwimmer or Aaron Sorkin have to say about Matthew Perry, rather than Matthew Perry. Plus, the truth is that The One About Matthew Perry almost isn’t about Matthew Perry at all, which I don’t really mean as a criticism, though it will leave some viewers disappointed. Yes, it contains a lot of the biographical details and memorable clips that you expect from a documentary about Perry. But The One About Matthew Perry might have been better if it had skipped the basics entirely, because it treats that stuff in a manner that feels perfunctory rather than even remotely inspired. It surely would have been more sharply focused. What, then, is The One About Matthew Perry ? It’s a sincere, generally non-exploitative examination of addiction and celebrity — but not from Perry’s perspective, since Perry wrote a bestselling memoir that covered all of that. Instead, it’s about addiction and celebrity as viewed from slightly outside the celebrity bubble. If Robertson had been able to trim The One About Matthew Perry down to a 100-minute feature-length doc that didn’t find the basics so necessary to include, it probably would have been a better project. I’m not sure I learned anything at all about Perry here, but the documentary’s heart is with the people still struggling with what they did or didn’t know and what they could or couldn’t do when it came to Perry’s life and death. Sure, it would be flashier if Netflix could boast that it had reunited the surviving cast of Friends , but most of The One About Matthew Perry is recounted by people you don’t know, starting with Mia Perry Bowick, Perry’s younger sister. Matthew Perry was 14 when she was born, and she did much of her growing up with an already famous sibling. The latter fact adds poignancy to her decision to become a psychotherapist, inspired by watching Matthew’s decades of struggles. Her memories of learning about Matthew’s first rehab stint from a tabloid headline, or of the day of her brother’s death, are heartbreaking — and not the sort of thing that will get aggregated in entertainment news stories. That’s why they cut through. The same is true of the recollections shared by Roger Castillo and David Pressman, friends going back to Perry’s earliest days struggling as an actor in Hollywood. I don’t know if Robertson reached out to Hank Azaria, part of the same group that hung out at Formosa Cafe and in various cheap Hollywood apartments. But again, it’s savvier to present this chapter of Perry’s life without the distraction of big names. Perry dated plenty of famous women, but the ex-girlfriends featured in the documentary aren’t the Lizzy Caplans or the Julia Robertses, but rather the René Ashtons and the Romes — women who knew Perry intimately but can speak without added distraction. (Actually, this stuff is already close to distracting. Ashton, in particularly, gives the impression that she’s trying to add sizzle to a documentary that doesn’t need it, but I’m glad she and Perry had sex on a private plane.) Instead of offering viewers a line-up of flashy tributes, Robertson wants viewers to come away thinking of Tim Harrington, who met Perry in recovery and ended up living at Perry’s house for a year; or West Huddleston, who worked with Perry on drug court advocacy campaigns. The thing viewers are supposed to take away from The One About Matthew Perry isn’t really that it’s hard to become famous and discover that fame (and $7 million) can’t cure the pernicious demons of addiction, but that it’s hard to do everything you can for a person and love them as best you’re able and still not be able to do enough. It’s hard to watch and painful to listen to, but Robertson handles the documentary’s key moments with subtlety and intimacy. There’s so much good stuff in The One About Matthew Perry that it’s unfortunate how often it’s lost underneath so much less interesting stuff. With all the people telling Perry stories that have never been heard before, do we really need the talk-show footage of Perry telling stories he told repeatedly? Probably not. Does Littlefield add anything that he didn’t say in his own book and that hasn’t been said in various documentaries about Friends ? No. Are the general platitudes about Perry’s talent and why Friends was successful — courtesy of a single cultural critic — really necessary? Maybe in principle, because you don’t want to just approach Perry in terms of his tragic end. But there had to be better ways of approaching the familiar side of things. There’s an original and insightful feature-length documentary that could have been chiseled out from under all the generic padding here. You can’t have the former without the latter, apparently. THR

title: The “Sukiyaki” Phenomenon: The Song Behind the Tokyo Film Festival’s Opening Movie
full_text: × Skip to main content By Gavin Blair Plus Icon Gavin Blair View All October 26, 2026 10:38pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Sukiyaki' Tokyo International Film Festival Opening the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival is Sukiyaki , Takahisa Zeze’s drama charting the backstory of the 1960s song that became a global hit and a symbol of Japan ’s recovery from postwar devastation and humiliation. Centered on composer and jazz pianist Hachidai Nakamura (Junichi Okada), the film tells of his partnership with lyricist Rokusuke Ei (Tori Matsuzaka), and how singer Kyu Sakamoto (Taiga Nakano) turned their combination of a jaunty melody and plaintive lyrics into an unlikely global pop culture phenomenon. Though the tale behind the tune was ripe for onscreen telling, the song’s legacy is perhaps even more remarkable. Related Stories Business Tokyo: TIFFCOM Market Chief On Riding the Japanese IP Wave as Entertainment Landscape Shifts Due to AI Movies Tokyo: Competition Jury Discusses Event's 'A-List' Status, Fighting Over Favorite Films An ill-fated recital left Nakamura struggling with debt and addiction as rockabilly eclipsed jazz. He was saved by forging an unlikely partnership with Ei, a radio writer who had never penned song lyrics, to write a rockabilly score for a 1959 movie from Toho (the company also distributing the 2026 film). In 1961, Nakamura and Ei wrote “ Ue o Muite Aruko “, which translates as ‘I look upwards as I walk,’ for which Nakamura incorporated traditional Japanese scales, jazz chords and U.S. pop influences. Ei’s melancholic lyrics were inspired by the failure of the mass Anpo protests to stop a Tokyo-Washington security treaty that maintained a huge American military presence in Japan, and the looking upwards in the song is to stop tears of sadness falling from his eyes. Singer Sakamoto was brought in on short notice for its premiere at Tokyo’s Sankei Hall on July 21, 1961 – only given the sheet music two hours beforehand. Unrehearsed, Sakamoto went into a minor key on an ad lib, sang the 4-beat song as an 8-beat, and came in a beat late, mimicking Japanese balladeers he had grown up listening to. These quirks added further layers to the song’s distinctiveness. Released as a single, it was the Music Life best domestic song from November 1961 to January 1962, selling 300,000 copies. Kyu Sakamoto on his global tour in 1963. Sjöberg Bildbyrå/ullstein bild via Getty Images It found its way overseas via Louis Benjamin of British label Pye Records visiting Japan in 1962 and falling for its catchy melody. He gave it to Kenny Ball and his Jazzmen to record an instrumental version titled “ Sukiyaki ,” which made the British top ten in February 1963. One story is that Benjamin came up with the name after eating sukiyaki, a hotpot dish, in Tokyo, while another version has Ball picking one of the only Japanese words he knew because he figured the original title was too difficult for listeners. After a U.S. release of Ball’s version, and another instrumental cover by Billy Vaughn, failed to make waves, Capitol US decided to gamble on the original Japanese version — but with the “Sukiyaki” title. It hit record stores on May 3, 1963 and in June topped the Billboard Hot 100 for three weeks. This made Sakamoto the only Japanese artist to ever have a U.S. No.1, and the song the first from Asia to do so. It would not be until BTS’s “Dynamite” in 2020 that another Asian artist would repeat that feat. The appeal of the infectious tune and Sakamoto’s whistling reached far beyond the U.S., with “Sukiyaki” topping rankings from Australia to Norway. The single eventually sold more than 13 million copies worldwide. As the Japanese public began to realize people around the world were whistling along to a song in their native tongue, Toshiba capitalized and reissued the single. The 1963 cover added “Sukiyaki” to the title, rendered in the katakana syllabary for foreign words, along with the packaging legend: “global hit!” Japan’s economy was by then registering double-digit growth as companies like Sony and Toyota were becoming global brands. The worldwide success of “Sukiyaki” was another source of pride for a national psyche still bruised by wartime defeat and occupation. International cover versions of “Sukiyaki” then came thick and fast, with dozens in Chinese languages alone, as well as interpretations in Spanish, German and French. Scores of Japanese artists have also covered the song. Among the U.S. fans of the 1963 release was a nine-year-old Janice-Marie Johnson, who later founded R&B and funk outfit A Taste of Honey. A few years after their No.1 hit Boogie Oogie Oogie , Johnson decided she wanted to do a version of “ Sukiyaki” and contacted lyricist Ei in Japan, who provided her with a rough English translation. She worked these into her own take on the song, but faced stiff opposition from her label and producer, who were convinced R&B audiences had no interest in Japanese-sounding music. Johnson’s persistence was justified when their “Sukiyaki” topped the Billboard R&B chart and reached number three on the Hot 100 in 1981. The band appeared alongside Sakamoto on Japanese TV. Johnson’s lyrics were used in hip-hop duo Doug E. Fresh & Slick Rick’s 1985 classic “ La Di Da Di .” On the evening of August 12, 1985 Sakamoto boarded Japan Air Lines flight 123 from Tokyo to Osaka. Twelve minutes after takeoff the Boeing 747 suffered catastrophic mechanical failure. The pilots managed to keep the plane in the air for around half an hour — enough time for many passengers to write messages to loved ones — before it crashed into a mountainside in central Japan, killing 520 of the 524 onboard, including Sakamoto. It remains the deadliest single-aircraft disaster in aviation history. Sakamoto’s song is played at the annual memorial service. “Sukiyaki” was revived as a symbol of melancholic hope in the wake of the 2011 earthquake, tsunami and nuclear disaster in Japan when it was sung by 71 celebrities in a television commercial. It was also featured in that year’s Ghibli movie From Up on Poppy Hill , leading to a reissue. Tokyo Ska Paradise Orchestra played it at the closing ceremony of the pandemic-delayed Tokyo Olympics in August 2021. Sukiyaki , the film, opens in Japan on Christmas Day, reuniting on screen the trio Sakamoto had said he wanted to bring back together just days before his death. title: Tokyo: TIFFCOM Market Chief On Riding the Japanese IP Wave as Entertainment Landscape Shifts Due to AI
full_text: × Skip to main content By Gavin J Blair Plus Icon Gavin J Blair View All October 26, 2026 9:51pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kaori Ikeda TIFFCOM As Tokyo International Film Festival has raised its game and its profile over recent years, its content market TIFFCOM has been carving out its own niche, bolstered by the attractiveness of Japanese IP. On top of attracting more exhibitors and visitors, the market has expanded its seminar offerings, landing bigger industry names to speak at them. In addition to the popularity of anime, the potential of manga and gameshow IP, and the success of Japan -related productions like Shōgun , interest in Japan itself is at an all-time high – nearly 43 million people visited last year. This concatenation of factors is delivering a boost to the fest and the market, acknowledges TIFFCOM managing director Kaori Ikeda. “It definitely is…Tokyo is probably one of the most fascinating cities in the world, and Japan is enjoying a boom. So definitely this supports our activities, because we are dealing with culture,” Ikeda tells The Hollywood Reporter as she and the TIFFCOM team were putting the final touches to preparations a few days before the market opens. Ikeda is in her third year as TIFFCOM managing director following a career with Japanese indie distributor Asmik Ace – where her acquisitions included Trainspotting and Dead Man Walking , “those kinds of good old ones” – a project with DreamWorks and five years at Japanese cable major J:COM. Among the initiatives she points to is the relaunch last year of Tokyo Story Market, which focused on book adaptation with Japanese publishing companies, as Tokyo IP Market: Adaptation & Remake, with a broader remit, this year bringing in remake-rights holders including film companies such as Toei and Shochiku, and toy company Takara Tomy. “This year Japan was the Country of Honour at the Cannes Marché du Film, which we collaborated with and took Tokyo IP Market there to introduce Japanese IP that could be adapted in various ways, into film, games or any other form,” says Ikeda, who emphasizes that it is being backed by major investment from the Japanese government and industry. Ikeda hails the Cannes venture a success that is likely to happen again, saying it brought together international producers and Japanese rights holders, and that she would like to include some smaller publishers which have limited experience in the global marketplace. TIFFCOM logged about 4,600 visitors and 300 exhibitors in 2025, up strongly from previous editions, and is on track to equal or exceed those figures this year. In line with the remake and co-production themes, the ‘Unlocking the Global Potential of Japanese IP’ session will feature producer Shinzo Matsuhashi ( Kokuhō , Kingdom ), Steven Maeda (Netflix’s One Piece ), and Amazon MGM Studios Japan head Buddy Marini. “And this year we are adding AI as a keynote. We have invited the executives from AGBO , Chris Brearton and Dominic Hughes for the Keynote: Technology and Storytelling, which we are very thrilled with,” adds Ikeda. The Association of Japanese Animations will again release its annual industry data at its TIFFCOM session, while TV stations will present case studies of overseas format sales. Another success story that Ikeda points to is the Tokyo Gap-Financing Market, now in its seventh year of linking partially funded projects with production partners. Two now completed productions from last year will be screened in this edition of the festival’s Crosscut Asia + section. Meanwhile, The Violinist , an animation which found an Italian partner at the 2023 event, took home the top award at Annecy this year, reports Ikeda proudly. All the while, the industry is shifting as are viewing habits. Short dramas are winning over audiences – not least in Japan – streamers recently seen as saviors are cutting budgets and AI is disrupting. “There are so many things happening in the market at the moment…So, we’re looking at how to be a better place for the industry to have business meetings and also to network,” adds Ikeda. TIFFCOM runs Oct. 28 to 30 at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center Hamamatsucho-kan. THR

title: Tokyo: Competition Jury Discusses Event’s ‘A-List’ Status, Fighting Over Favorite Films
full_text: × Skip to main content By Abid Rahman Plus Icon Abid Rahman International Editor, Digital gentlemanabroad Follow Sign Up View All October 26, 2026 8:29pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tokyo Film Festival competition jury. From left: Oh Jungwan, Rolf de Heer, Watanabe Makiko and Yov Moor. Tokyo International Film Festival A lively discussion about the global standing of the Tokyo International Film Festival — and whether such considerations even matter — was the highlight of a rather genteel competition jury press conference on Tuesday. The 2026 Tokyo competition jury is headed by Dutch-Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer ( Bad Boy Bubby, Charlie’s Country, Ten Canoes and The Tracker ), and he was joined on stage by competition jury members: French film colorist and producer Yov Moor; leading South Korean producer Oh Jungwan; veteran Japanese actress Makiko Watanabe; and Taiwanese-American producer Alex C. Lo. Related Stories Music Macklemore Launches Sold-Out Free Palestine Tour in Dublin With Hozier, Kneecap and Ed Sheeran's Backing Band Business Disney+ to Add Channel 4 Network and On-Demand Content in U.K., Ireland Under "Most Ambitious" EMEA Deal Yet In stark contrast to many recent pressers at the major European and American film festivals, the Tokyo jury conversation was largely politics free, though the event kicked off with an amusingly blunt answer from De Heer as to why there aren’t more Australian and Japanese co-productions. De Heer was asked about the conspicuous lack of co-productions between Australia and Japan , despite both countries having strong state backing to film production. “It makes no sense for a Japanese film to shoot in Australia, or it makes no sense for an Australian film to shoot in Japan,” said De Heer. “Europe is very good at doing co-productions strictly on a financial basis, really. Australia is not so good at that. The sort of co-productions that work out of Australia are ones that are natural—that have a natural story where some things need to be shot in Japan, some things need to be shot in Australia. Those will always be possible if the scripts come and if they’re right.” After the jury members spoke about their great honor at being invited to oversee this year’s competition, the conversation became a touch more animated when they were asked about the standing of Tokyo Film Festival , as compared to other international festivals, and specifically about Tokyo’s recent inclusion as an “A-list” event by the International Federation of Film Producers Associations (FIAPF). “I think Tokyo was… has always been considered one of those festivals by most people who attend festivals,” said De Heer. “Tokyo was effectively an ‘A’ festival. And so in that sense, I don’t think it makes a lot of difference. This sort of categorization seems to be becoming more important in terms of the quality of films available to that festival, and so in that sense it may help that it is officially now again an ‘A’, but I don’t think it changes the festival so much.” “I think Rolf’s answer is… is enough for… is not enough for you?” said Oh to laughter in the room. “Actually, I don’t know about that. I’m not a film festival person, so I don’t know what is A-list or not. Probably A-list means good! But as an audience, we’re not going to the festival because of their A-list or not. We just go to watch film and enjoy the festival feeling.” Asked whether the tier system was somewhat redundant nowadays, De Heer replied cryptically, “It matters a great deal to some people, and not at all to others. And that is as it should be.” From left: Yov Moor, Oh Jungwan, Rolf de Heer, Makiko Watanabe and Alex C. Lo. Tokyo International Film Festival Later in the discussion, Lo returned to the status of Tokyo, suggesting the festival’s reputation was built upon two key operational traits: world-leading festival hospitality and an exceptionally attentive, intellectually curious audience that respects original storytelling. Looking ahead to the competition for the Tokyo Grand Prix, the jury also discussed how they would handle disagreements over the 15 films selected to compete. “It depends entirely on the very specific situation—how much disagreement, how divided is the jury,” said De Heer. “I don’t think there is an answer to that until we get to that point. As far as I understand it, I’m with four other very reasonable people, and I’m sure we can find a way through so that we don’t end up with some sort of lesser compromise film, but a really interesting film that maybe some of us don’t like.” Oh added jokingly that she was ready to fight De Heer over the selection. “Sometimes you want to fight for the film,” she added. “I had an experience where I fought for 7 hours with another jury! Every other jury member hated me. [laughter] But we are grownups and there are so many good films, so we will find a good way to compromise. I hope I don’t fight with him for 7 hours this time!” Elsewhere, Moor spoke of his delight at being invited to sit on the jury, especially given film colorists are often overlooked for such roles. “When I received the invitation I was very surprised, because [with] my job [as a colorist] it [is] quite rare to receive this kind of invitation. And for me… now I’m almost two years in Tokyo… for me it was a very great surprise, and also for people who do the same job as me, to be able to be a jury at a film festival.” Moor added, “For me, it’s like a little dream, and also maybe to try to show more of my job as a colorist—not only me, but people who do the same job as me.” De Heer, in his taciturn manner, also spoke about his future plans. Asked about his next film, the director said, “I don’t know… I am in-between, and I’m trying to make decisions about what to do.” He added, “This is another good reason why I enjoy being here, because it is a punctuation point. It’s not a very good answer for you, but it is the answer.” THR

title: Parallax Films Boards Sales On ‘Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting’ Ahead of Tokyo World Premiere
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Rolf de Heer & Fellow Tokyo Jury Members Talk Festival ‘A-List’ Ratings, Co-Production & How To Judge Films Parallax Films Boards Sales On ‘Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting’ Ahead of Tokyo World Premiere Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi Pledges Support For Japanese Film At Tokyo Fest Opening View All October 26, 2026 4:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting Parallax Films EXCLUSIVE: Parallax Films has boarded international sales for Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting , directed by Chinese artist-filmmaker Qiu Jiongjiong, which is receiving its world premiere in the main competition section of Tokyo International Film Festival. Qiu is known internationally for his debut narrative feature A New Old Play , which won the Special Jury Prize at the 2021 Locarno Film Festival. Rooted in the folklore of China’s Sichuan province, Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting unfolds through four separate feasts spanning four millennia, that “bring the living and the dead, gods and ghosts, to the same table”. The word “fuxi” in its title is a Sichuan expression meaning “the joy of the belly”. Related Stories News Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi Pledges Support For Japanese Film At Tokyo Fest Opening News How TIFFCOM Is Building On Cannes Recognition To Strengthen Global Networks, Co-Production & Japanese IP Parallax describes the film as a “handcrafted mythic fantasy” referencing Qiu’s unique style of filmmaking that combines painting, theatre and cinema. “Rather than reproducing reality, Qiu uses hand-painted scenic flats, handmade props and theatrical staging to give physical form to his imagination, creating a cinematic universe entirely his own,” Parallax explains. ( See here for the trailer of the film.) Watch on Deadline The cast includes Lee Kang-sheng, Taiwanese filmmaker Tsai Ming-liang’s longtime leading actor, playing two grandmothers in different chapters of the film, marking his first female roles on screen. He is joined by actor-filmmaker Lee Hong-chi, whose directorial debut Love Is A Gun won the Lion of the Future award at Venice, and Annie Chen, known for her role in Netflix series Born For The Spotlight . Produced by David Tang, Ningyuan Ding and Zhao Jin, Fuxi is a co-production between Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. The project received support from international film funds and project markets including Hong Kong-Asia Film Financing Forum (HAF), MPA APSA Academy Film Fund, Red Sea Fund, Doha Film Institute and Network of Asian Fantastic Films (NAFF) at Korea’s Bucheon International Fantastic Film Festival. The film’s visual world also extends beyond the screen in Fuxi: A Feast For The Universe , Qiu’s large-scale solo exhibition at A4 Art Museum in Chengdu. Bringing together paintings, sets, props and installations, the exhibition translates the film’s imagined universe into a new spatial narrative. The deal for world sales on Fuxi extends Parallax’s relationship with Qiu, with the company also representing his seven previous films, which include A New Old Play, experimental documentary shorts and documentary features. title: Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max BAFTA Names New Chair Stephen & Simon Cornwell Take On Chairmen Roles At ‘Night Manager’ Producer The Ink Factory As Michele Wolkoff Upped To President Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK View All October 26, 2026 5:01pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Daisy Haggard and Bella Ramsey in the upcoming 'Maya' Channel 4 Disney and Channel 4 have struck a landmark UK content deal that will also see the Channel 4 linear network become available on Disney+ , a UK first. In one of the biggest deals of its kind in UK TV history, shows like Channel 4 stalwart Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins and upcoming Bella Ramsey-starrer Maya will drop on Disney+ at the start of next year in the UK and Ireland. From there, Disney+ EMEA general manager Karl Holmes told Deadline there will be a “regular tempo” of new Channel 4 shows entering the Mouse House, although he wouldn’t put an exact figure on this. Related Stories Cancellations and Renewals 'Coven Academy' Renewed For Season 2 By Disney News Nicola Coughlan's 'I Am Helen' Trailer Shows Dark Side Of Modern Relationships As Toxic Masculinity Takes Its Toll From the start of next year, Disney+ UK and Ireland subs will be able to watch these shows day-and-date plus hundreds of hours of on-demand content like Russell T. Davies’ Tip Toe and Nicola Coughlan’s Big Mood. And in a UK first, Channel 4’s linear channel will also become available in its entirety on Disney+. Watch on Deadline Speaking alongside Holmes, Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra claimed the Gogglebox network and Disney+ don’t have much overlap in terms of audience and the deal can be complementary. Channel 4 already licenses Disney content like Abbott Elementary , The X Files and Scandal for its VoD player. “From our perspective, people develop viewing habits in different places,” said Dogra. “There are a number of services they may use to discover content, and we need to make sure Channel 4 is available on those platforms.” Holmes said Disney+ viewing skews younger than public service broadcasters like Channel 4, adding that around 40% of Disney+ viewing over the past year has come from 16-34 year olds. “There is a genuinely complementary relationship here,” added Holmes. “We’re not competing with free-to-air partners; we’re helping them reach a broader audience.” The news comes more than a year after Disney+ kicked off a strategy of partnering with local European networks by striking a content-swapping deal with ITV that has seen shows like The Bear and The Kardashians head to ITVX, while Love Island and Mr Bates vs the Post Office went in the opposite direction. This preceded Disney deals with the likes of Germany’s ZDF and Spain’s Atresmedia. Netflix has simultaneously struck a high-profile pact with France’s TF1 that was recently talked up by Ted Sarandos. Holmes said the Disney-Channel 4 pact is broader in scope than Disney-ITV and his team learned from the latter when executing the former. “One clear lesson is that a focus on shows that are current, big, bold and buzzy – and available day-and-date – works particularly well with our audience,” he added. “That’s what we’ve prioritised in this collaboration. We’d like to build on it further in the future.” For Dogra, who has been in post less than a year, the deal is the latest landmark agreement she has helped mastermind following the once-in-a-generation ads deal inked with Paramount (now Skydance) UK network 5 . She has talked up collaboration opportunites including putting Channel 4 shows on BBC iPlayer , while downplaying the idea of a BBC-Channel 4 merger. While the Paramount deal “gives us scale from an advertising perspective,” today’s agreement “allows us to maximise our impact by reaching as many people as possible across the UK and Ireland, including people who may not currently be using Channel 4 services,” Dogra added. “The premise is that we need to lean into the wider ecosystem,” said the CEO, a former Sky and Warner Bros. Discovery executive. “We’re not going to build scale in every area ourselves, so we need to work with like-minded organizations.” More details on the Disney-Channel 4 deal will be incoming in due course. Hooper led publicity, awards and creative marketing operations, earning the studio 21 Best Picture Oscar nominations — including Best Picture winners Slumdog Millionaire , 12 Years a Slave , Birdman , The Shape of Water and Nomadland ; a total of 183 Oscar nominations; and 49 wins. Related Stories News Disney Hit By Layoffs, A Couple Hundred Workers Cut News Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK As far as Golden Globes go, her work delivered 32 awards from 133 nominations, including 20 Best Picture noms and eight wins. Hooper, who joined Searchlight in 2006, is respected by her peers for her taste, whip-smart instincts, creativity and ingenuity in marketing, and was internally known as “the closer,” bringing a film’s campaign home in its final stretch. Her campaigns for various Oscar winners often dialed into the cultural zeitgeist, from understanding how Nomadland would resonate in the context of the pandemic, to spotting the cultural relevance of Slumdog Millionaire in the Obama era, and appreciating the historical significance of 12 Years a Slave , which was closely followed by Birdman. This season, Hooper’s awards campaigns include for Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine (93% certified fresh) and Tony Gilroy’s Behemoth! (87% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes). Watch on Deadline Prior to joining Searchlight, Hooper spent four years at Fox Broadcasting where she was VP of Entertainment Publicity. While at Fox, Hooper spearheaded the implementation of national publicity campaigns for multiple series such as launching American Idol , 24 , Arrested Development , Family Guy and The Simpsons . Prior to joining Fox, Hooper was the Director of Entertainment Communications at CBS Entertainment in New York, where she was part of the team that launched and created the publicity campaign for Survivor . After Disney acquired 20th Century Fox in March 2019, Hooper made the jump. I understand that Hooper’s departure is part of the cuts that occurred at the Disney studio earlier this month. Other notable releases during Hooper’s Searchlight administration include James Mangold’s eight-time Oscar-nominated A Complete Unknown, starring Timothée Chalamet as Bob Dylan; Jesse Eisenberg’s A Real Pain , which won an Oscar for Kieran Culkin; Marielle Heller’s Nightbitch starring Amy Adams; Yorgos Lanthimos’ four-time Academy Award winner Poor Things, starring and produced by Emma Stone; Lanthimos’ follow-up Kinds of Kindness , also starring Stone with Jesse Plemons, Hong Chau and Margaret Qualley; and Andrew Haigh’s romantic drama All of Us Strangers starring Andrew Scott, Paul Mescal, Jamie Bell and Claire Foy. She also oversaw the marketing on streaming originals such as Tina Mabry’s The Supremes at Earl’s All-You-Can-Eat starring Uzo Aduba, Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor and Sanaa Lathan; Karrie Crouse and Will Joines’ Hold Your Breath starring Sarah Paulson; and Eva Longoria’s Oscar-nominated Flamin’ Hot , which became the first original film to debut simultaneously on both Hulu and Disney+ and is Searchlight’s most-watched streaming motion picture of all time. Other past successful films during Hooper’s reign include The Favourite, Can You Ever Forgive Me?, Isle of Dogs, Super Troopers 2, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, Gifted, Jackie, Brooklyn, Wild, The Grand Budapest Hotel, Beasts of the Southern Wild, The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel, The Descendants, The Tree of Life, Black Swan, 127 Hours, Crazy Heart, 500 Days of Summer, The Wrestler, Juno, Once, Little Miss Sunshine and The Last King of Scotland. Hooper shared the Publicist Guild of America’s Maxwell Weinberg Showmanship Award for her work on Survivor . She is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and BAFTA. title: Milcho Manchevski Talks ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover’, His Second Feature Of 2026 & Exposing Corruption At Macedonia’s Film Agency — Tokyo
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Bill Kramer Says AMPAS Plans To Expand List Of Festivals That Can Serve As Qualifiers For The International Oscar Category Milcho Manchevski Talks ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover’, His Second Feature Of 2026 & Exposing Corruption At Macedonia’s Film Agency — Tokyo Janus Films Acquires Alfonso Cuarón’s ‘Y Tu Mamá También’ Ahead Of 25th Anniversary 4K Re-Release View All October 26, 2026 5:48pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tokyo Film Festival. This week, Macedonian filmmaker Milcho Manchevski returns with Sister Brother Manhole Cover , his second feature of the year, which screens in competition at the Tokyo Film Festival. Directed by Manchevski from a screenplay he also wrote, Sister Brother Manhole Cover follows siblings Malina and Viktor, who live on the outskirts of post-Communist Macedonia. They make their living stealing bronze busts and manhole covers, which line their city’s streets. When a routine theft goes wrong and Viktor is badly injured, Malina strikes a desperate deal with a corrupt doctor, forcing them into a dangerous journey through Macedonia’s underworld. Their journey leads to an unexpected refuge: the opulent home of the doctor’s blind mother. Related Stories News Parallax Films Boards Sales On 'Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting' Ahead of Tokyo World Premiere News Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi Pledges Support For Japanese Film At Tokyo Fest Opening Sister Brother Manhole Cover is Manchevski’s ninth feature. The filmmaker debuted his first documentary, Good People , earlier this year at the Sarajevo Film Festival. Watch on Deadline “It’s unusual to have two films come out at the same time, but better two than zero,” Manchevski joked in an interview with Deadline ahead of his trip to Tokyo for Sister Brother, adding that he is enjoying this productive period after spending many years being barred from producing films in his home country. Manchevski, who won the Golden Lion at Venice with his debut feature Before the Rain (1994), was blacklisted and had several projects halted by the Macedonian Film Agency after he reported corruption at the organization. Manchevski’s accusations were later upheld by Macedonia’s Anti-Corruption Commission after an investigation. Below, the veteran filmmaker, who lives between New York and Macedonia, speaks with Deadline about the extensive witch hunt he endured after exposing corruption at the Macedonian Film Agency, finally getting to make Sister Brother Manhole Cover, and why he believes the Tokyo Film Festival is the perfect launchpad for movies. Sister Brother Manhole Cover is a Banana Film production, in co-production with Gala Film (Bulgaria), Sense Production (Serbia), Tirana Film Institute (Albania), Berkeley Media Group (UK), Amarcord Production in association with Augustus Color (Italy) with the support of North Macedonia Film Agency, the Bulgarian National Film Center, Film Center Serbia, the Albanian National Center of Cinematography, and Italy’s Direzione Generale Cinema e Audiovisivo – Ministero della Cultura. The Rome-based Coccinelle Film is handling world sales on the title. DEADLINE: Milcho, where did this idea come from? MILCHO MANCHEVSKI: I wanted to make a film about sisterly and brotherly love—something we rarely see in movies or even in literature. It was also partly inspired by Macedonian folk songs and folk literature, which often include the theme of sisterly love. Sometimes it turns shocking and dark, but it is always fully dedicated. That was the initial embryo. Then I wanted to talk about inequality and wealth inequality. I think that’s the premier issue of today. So many problems in the world go back to this sense of unfairness and inequality. That feeling festers in people. But I didn’t want to turn it into an exclusively dark story. I thought it should be told through defiance and humor, because Victor and Marlena don’t see themselves as victims. They see themselves as people with agency—people who do things. Unfortunately, pretty much the only thing they can do is petty crime. DEADLINE: Yeah, I loved the idea of people stealing the busts. It’s so European. MANCHEVSKI: People actually do it. It’s three euros a kilo for the metal. I did a little research. There was an explosion of new monuments in Macedonia in the early 2010s, because the nationalist government decided to reintroduce us to our past. There was plenty of cash just lying around. And the manhole covers, they cover the underground and the septic part of us that we don’t really want to smell or see. Then our heroes take them off, and you can smell the reek. DEADLINE: I read this film was previously titled Leaving Copacabana? MANCHEVSKI: Yes. The title was Leaving Copacabana . Copacabana was their slum, which we constructed for the film. The little shacks you see are leaning on an ancient aqueduct. We got permission from the government to work there because it’s a national monument. We constructed the shacks for two reasons: first, to have full control; and second, so we wouldn’t go into somebody’s home—somebody’s slum—and disrupt their life. The slum was jokingly called Copacabana, as if they were in Brazil. The tagline was “sister, brother, manhole cover.” But that title somehow took over because it’s more irreverent and catchier, and I think it describes the film better. It’s not so much about leaving one place and going to a richer place; it’s about their relationship and society. DEADLINE: Where did you shoot this film? There are a lot of locations. MANCHEVSKI: Everything was done on location. There was no studio. And even on location, we didn’t want to change too much. The exception was the slum, which we constructed based on actual slums in Skopje. Most are inhabited by Roma, but not exclusively. We built it around the aqueduct because I liked the graphic quality, but also because it incorporated the ancient past into the very prosaic present of the characters and the whole community. Everything else was scouted around Skopje. We looked for actual places that had a certain smell, places where you could feel the underbelly, but also places that could give us a cross-section of society. For example, you have the illegal dump, which we had to sanitize so people could work there. DEADLINE: That was a real dump? MANCHEVSKI: That was a real dump. We took over a corner of it, sanitized the area, and brought in our own paper and cloth—things that didn’t stink too much. We had to ward off dogs. We liked that particular dump because you could see the highway below. Again, there was this contrast: here and there, us and them. That’s necessary when you’re telling a drama. The house was a real house, too. We didn’t do much to it; we brought in the piano and the busts, which we created, of course. I’m taking one of the manhole covers to the red carpet in Tokyo next week. DEADLINE: You’ve become a regular at Tokyo Film Festival. Why do you screen your films here? MANCHEVSKI: It’s an old love story. Before the Rain , my first film, played Tokyo. Going there and spending time there was so nice. I like how people in Japan, and especially at the festival, appreciate films. They take special care with them; they create new posters and trailers. It’s not just a run-of-the-mill place or festival. Then Dust played there, and then Kaymak . Now, I want to go there—it is at the top of my list. DEADLINE: This is your second film of the year. You were in Sarajevo with the doc Good People. I read that this was mostly because for years you were unable to produce anything? MANCHEVSKI: Yes, for a while, I wasn’t able to work because I reported corruption at the film agency in Macedonia. I did it twice, and it was eventually confirmed by the Anti-Corruption Commission and the State Audit Office. As retaliation, they blacklisted me, filed criminal charges against me, launched a smear campaign, and blocked my previous films and films in progress. Eventually I won two court cases against the agency, and the dam broke. This film was initially approved in 2022, and then, at the same time, the tragedy in Kočani happened. I felt I should make a documentary about it. The two films are completely different stylistically. There’s a lot of humor in Sister Brother ; there’s no humor in Good People . It’s somber, with a glimmer of hope at the end. The overlap mostly happened in the edit, where you can shuttle between the two. I know it’s unusual to have two films come out at the same time, but better two than zero. DEADLINE: You’ve worked across the United States and Europe and have been able to make many different kinds of things. Many European and American filmmakers now talk about how difficult it is to make work. How do you feel about the industry today? MANCHEVSKI: I’m always an outsider, and I like it that way. I’ve lived in New York since 1985, but recently I’ve mostly been making films in Europe because of the general attitude toward filmmaking and the arts. Financing is always tough. It’s the curse of filmmaking. I’m jealous of painters and poets: you sit down, do your work, and it’s done. Maybe nobody will see it or like it, but at least it’s finished. With film, you first have to sell it and then make it. Filmmaking involves a lot of money, technology, and egos. Working in Europe has advantages, but distribution is not as muscular as in Hollywood. But nobody tells you how to end the film, whom to cast, or whether you need to reshoot a scene. You want feedback and collaboration, but it’s not a situation where the money dictates what the art will look like. That’s why I prefer Europe to Hollywood. I’ve worked in the United States—I worked on The Wire for HBO, made an independent film, developed films with studios, and even started a studio film. But in the last decade or so, there has been pressure to conform ideologically and make films with messages. I think every film has a message by default. The question is whether it offers more: Is there beauty in the film? Is there something profound? Does it talk about a bigger truth rather than just a message? The pressure—from festivals and film funds—to be message-driven and ideological comes at the expense of everything else. Even when I agree with the message, it’s a pity that so much contemporary cinema turns into two-dimensional pamphlets. Having repeatedly told Trump to keep his MAGA mitts off his classic Rockin’ in the Free World song, the 80-year-old Grandfather of Grunge took the poll struggling POTUS back to court today with new $10 million copyright infringement suit. And, as Young always does on the guitar, the two time Rock & Roll Hall of Famer let Trump have it. “ Rockin’ in the Free World is a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten,” the short but sharp complaint says. “The lyrics paint vivid street-level portraits – a mother discarding her baby, addicts lost in despair, garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity – while the repeated chorus delivers a savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn’t shared by all. In short, the Song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for.” Related Stories News CNN And Politico Again Are Barred From Air Force One Politics 'Smear' Campaign: George Clooney, Betty Gilpin, Adam Scott & Laverne Cox Team To Read Clark Gregg-Penned Political Play As Midterms Fundraiser Trump first used the 1991 hit back at the very start of his first serious (semi-serious?) White House run in 2015. Young told him to back off then and told Trump to back off again in 2020 with legal action. As Young’s critiques of Trump got louder and louder in song and from the stage, it seemed the 45th and now 47th President, or at least his attorneys, got it — until October 12. in Youngstown, Ohio. Watch on Deadline The the five-page filing in federal court in Virginia states: “Just prior to Donald J. Trump taking the stage to speak at the Youngstown Rally, the Committee caused Rockin’ in the Free World to be played. On information and belief, the Committee has caused the Song to be played numerous times at other rallies designed to encourage Republican votes in the upcoming mid-term elections.” As today made clear, you don’t mess with old Neil and you don’t break your word to him. “Donald J. Trump (‘Trump’) is now and at the time of all rallies this year was personally aware that a license would be required to play the Song at rallies and that Young has not, and would not, grant the required license,” proclaims the complaint. “In 2020 Young sued another corporation formed by Trump, Donald J. Trump For President, Inc., for copyright infringement of Rockin’ in the Free World along with another song written by Young,” the document by lawyers Scott Simmons and Robert Besser against Trump 47 Committee Inc. adds. “Donald J Trump For President, Inc. asserted no defense and immediately settled shortly after it was served, promising that it would never again use Rockin’ in the Free World without a license and permission from Young.” The White House did not respond to Deadline’s request for comment on the complaint. On the other hand, the Neil Young, or at least his lawyers couldn’t resist a bit of wit, or at least a legalese laugh at Trump’s expense — and maybe even their own. “Young has suffered damage to his reputation and brand as a result of the implication that he supports Donald J. title: Rolf de Heer & Fellow Tokyo Jury Members Talk Festival ‘A-List’ Ratings, Co-Production & How To Judge Films
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Rolf de Heer & Fellow Tokyo Jury Members Talk Festival ‘A-List’ Ratings, Co-Production & How To Judge Films Parallax Films Boards Sales On ‘Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting’ Ahead of Tokyo World Premiere Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi Pledges Support For Japanese Film At Tokyo Fest Opening View All October 26, 2026 9:40pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Yov Moor, Oh Jungwan, Rolf de Heer, Makiko Watanabe, Alex Lo Deadline Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer , president of the competition jury at this year’s Tokyo International Film Festival, talked about the significance of ‘A-list’ ratings for film festivals at the jury press conference today. Tokyo has recently had its status as an A-list festival reaffirmed by the Fédération Internationale des Associations des Producteurs de Films (FIAPF), a Brussels-based global organization that rates film festivals. But the practice of rating festivals, and the process and criteria for rating them, has proved controversial over the years. Related Stories News Milcho Manchevski Talks 'Sister Brother Manhole Cover', His Second Feature Of 2026 & Exposing Corruption At Macedonia's Film Agency -- Tokyo News Parallax Films Boards Sales On 'Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting' Ahead of Tokyo World Premiere In March this year, FIAPF overhauled its festival accreditation system for the first time since 2007, with a new framework that classifies 17 festivals as “A-list” and expanding the overall number of accredited festivals around the world. Five of these festivals are based in the Asia Pacific region, including Tokyo, Busan, IFFI Goa, Cairo and Shanghai. When asked about the ratings system, De Heer said: “Tokyo has always been considered an A-list festival by most people who attend festivals, so in that sense I don’t think it makes a lot of difference. This sort of categorization seems to be becoming more important in terms of the quality of films that are available to a festival, so in that sense it may help that Tokyo now officially has that rating again, but I don’t think it changes the festival so much.” Watch on Deadline FIAPF’s old system classified festivals in four groups: competitive, specialized, non-competitive and documentary and short film festivals. The 2026 reform collapsed the four categories into one group of 49 accredited festivals across 29 countries on five continents. When pushed on the subject with another question, De Heer said: “It matters a great deal to some people and not at all to others, and that is at it should be.” De Heer is heading the main competition jury at this year’s Tokyo film festival , along with Korean producer Oh Jungwan, New York and Tokyo-based producer Alex C. Lo, French colorist Yov Moor and Japanese actress Makiko Watanabe. The jury also talked about international co-productions, as several films in this year’s line-up of 15 competition titles have been structured this way. Lo agreed with a question from the audience about the growing trend: “I didn’t notice there’s an increasing number of co-productions in the festival line-up, but it’s true that a lot of producers in Europe, US and the rest of the world are increasingly seeking co-production opportunities, mainly due to the link to their local government production support.” When asked about the potential for co-productions between Japan and Australia, De Heer noted that the Australian film industry does not approach co-production in the same way as European producers: “It makes no sense for a Japanese film to shoot in Australia, and it makes no sense for an Australian film to shoot in Japan. Europe is very good at doing co-productions only on a financial basis. Australia is not so good at that. “The sort of co-productions that work out of Australia have a natural story where some things need to be shot in Japan, some things in Australia. Those will always be possible if the scripts come and if they’re right.” The jury also talked about their criteria for judging the 15 films in competition, which includes titles from across Europe and the Asia Pacific region. Oh Jungwan said: “For me as a jury member, I’m looking at whether I’m convinced by the story the director is telling and the way he’s telling it.” She later said she’s also prepared to fight for the films she loves and once had a seven-hour discussion about a film when serving on another jury. Yov Moor said: “When watching each film, I’m looking at what is interesting and sincere in the film, but also really trying to imagine what the next film of this director could be.” Makiko Watanabe added: “I try to see films without any preconceived notions and don’t try to look for answers while watching. As jury, there are other things we need to look at, but mostly I’ll look for what touches me and later digest what I took from the film.” Tokyo International Film Festival opened last night and runs for ten days in the Hibiya-Ginza district of Tokyo. It closes on November 4 with the awards ceremony and a screening of Korean filmmaker Yeon Sang-ho’s Colony. title: Bill Kramer Says AMPAS Plans To Expand List Of Festivals That Can Serve As Qualifiers For The International Oscar Category
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Bill Kramer Says AMPAS Plans To Expand List Of Festivals That Can Serve As Qualifiers For The International Oscar Category Milcho Manchevski Talks ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover’, His Second Feature Of 2026 & Exposing Corruption At Macedonia’s Film Agency — Tokyo Janus Films Acquires Alfonso Cuarón’s ‘Y Tu Mamá También’ Ahead Of 25th Anniversary 4K Re-Release View All October 26, 2026 10:39pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bill Kramer AMPS The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences will expand the list of festivals that can serve as standalone qualifiers for the International Film Oscar category, AMPAS CEO Bill Kramer confirmed this morning during an interview with Deadline at the Tokyo Film Festival. Related Stories News Oscars 2027 International Feature Film Submissions By Country: UK, Argentina, Iran, Rwanda Among Latest To Declare Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Guilds & More Kramer, who has become a frequent fixture on the international festival circuit in recent years, is at Tokyo alongside AMPAS President Lynette Howell Taylor and Chief Membership, Impact and Industry Officer Meredith Shea to take part in a series of public talks titled Academy in Tokyo. The sessions are one of the headline events this year at the Tokyo Film Festival . Kramer will also receive an honorary leadership award. Ahead of the festivities, Kramer sat down with Deadline in Tokyo. “Our plan is to expand the number of festivals,” Kramer told Deadline when asked about the list of festivals that can serve as feeders for the International Oscar category. Currently, under the rules introduced in May, films that win the top award at Berlin, Busan, Cannes, Sundance, Toronto, and Venice can be automatically submitted for the international category alongside films chosen by a country’s official submission committee. Watch on Deadline Kramer continued: “We started with six festivals because we wanted to make sure there were juried awards, which not every festival has.” Kramer added that the new rule is part of the Academy’s plan to globalize its efforts and approach the international category in a “more holistic way.” “A few years ago, the first thing we did was create a rule allowing refugee filmmakers who are no longer in their home country to have their films submitted by a host-country committee,” Kramer said. “That was the first step in creating a broader aperture for who can participate in the category. The next step was to consider how we could select films beyond committee-selected submissions and ensure greater global representation.” Kramer said AMPAS remains in constant conversation with film festivals across the globe. “We want to make sure there is proper global representation in the number of festivals we’re working with for this category,” he said. “It’s all about inviting more films into the conversation.” On the topic of international, Kramer said 25% of the Academy’s membership now resides outside the United States—a natural reflection, he believes, of global shifts in film production and consumption. “I think the lines between U.S. and non-U.S. cinema, first-run and classic films, animation, and documentaries have become much less distinct,” he said. “A lot of this has to do with the pandemic, when people at home watched films they normally wouldn’t have watched—young people especially. It changed the nature of our industry.” Kramer said the Academy’s increasing global makeup is one of the main factors that makes YouTube the most appropriate broadcast home for the Oscars moving forward. It was announced in December 2025 that YouTube won the rights to host the Academy Awards starting in 2029. The Google-owned service outbid other offers, including one from the Oscars’ longtime home ABC, which has been hosting the event since 1976. Disney’s deal runs through 2028. YouTube’s first show will be the 101st Oscars ceremony, and its deal will run through 2033. “The beauty of the YouTube deal is that everyone will see the same show,” he said. “We’ll have control over fan engagement and reach 2.5 billion people around the world at the same time, on the same night, in more than 30 languages. It also gives us more quality control over what our fans see and experience. That’s really important.” YouTube’s deal for the Oscars has been one of the biggest shifts as streaming platforms take on more live events. Netflix has the SAG Awards, now renamed The Actor Awards, and Prime Video will broadcast the Emmys from 2027. But the alliance between big tech and the film world hasn’t been without substantial friction; take Amazon’s mishandling of Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial . When asked whether the Academy has planned for similar scenarios, Kramer concluded: “There’s no censorship allowed at the Academy, at the Oscars, or on our broadcast. We’ve been very clear about that, and Google and YouTube completely understand.” The Tokyo Film Festival runs until November 4.
